subtopic: REPORTED U.S. OBJECTION TO CANADA-RUSSIA AGREEMENT

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: REPORTED U.S. OBJECTION TO CANADA-RUSSIA AGREEMENT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would ask the Secretary of State for External Affairs whether there is any basis for press reports to the effect that President Johnson, or someone on his behalf, raised strong objections to Canada signing an air agreement with the Soviet union or Soviet government. When were those representations made, and were any of them in writing?

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Marlin (Secrelary of Slate for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: REPORTED U.S. OBJECTION TO CANADA-RUSSIA AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Can-ada-U.S.S.R. air agreement, copies of which were tabled in the house yesterday afternoon, provides for air service between Moscow and Montreal only. It is expected that both Air
Canada and Aeroflot will fly one round trip per week between these two cities, but there is no question in the agreement of an extension to other points.
So far as I am aware the United States is not opposed to this agreement. Indeed, hon. members may recall that in 1961 the United States negotiated a somewhat similar agreement with the Soviet union, although this has not yet been brought into effect.
In any event, the agreement signed yesterday by the Canadian government is based on decisions taken by the Canadian government.

subtopic: REPORTED U.S. OBJECTION TO CANADA-RUSSIA AGREEMENT
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: REPORTED U.S. OBJECTION TO CANADA-RUSSIA AGREEMENT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the question I asked was whether objections had been raised by President Johnson or someone on his behalf, and it requires just a simple answer. If such did not take place then surely a negative answer would be the answer, rather than a generality.

subtopic: REPORTED U.S. OBJECTION TO CANADA-RUSSIA AGREEMENT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have not used generalities in my response. I have given a pretty detailed reply to most of what my right hon. friend asked-

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: REPORTED U.S. OBJECTION TO CANADA-RUSSIA AGREEMENT
speechtext: Most of it.

subtopic: REPORTED U.S. OBJECTION TO CANADA-RUSSIA AGREEMENT
speechtext:
-but since my right hon. friend reminds that he had another aspect to his question I might as well address myself to that.
As my right hon. friend knows, it is not normal to confirm or deny whether exchanges of communications between heads of government have taken place on any particular subject. Such communications are privileged. Of course there has been an opportunity not only for the United States but for other countries to express their views, but I would repeat that the agreement signed yesterday, so far as I am concerned and so far as I know, is not opposed by the United States. I also added that in any event the decision taken was a decision taken by the government of Canada.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: REPORTED U.S. OBJECTION TO CANADA-RUSSIA AGREEMENT
speechtext:
If there was not any
objection, wherein did the courage consist?

subtopic: REPORTED U.S. OBJECTION TO CANADA-RUSSIA AGREEMENT
speechtext:
In replying to my
right hon. friend.

subtopic: REPORTED U.S. OBJECTION TO CANADA-RUSSIA AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: On the orders of the day:

maintopic: LAOS-REPORTED BOMBINGS BY U.S. AIR FORCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I direct a question to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. In view of reports from Saigon to the effect that for several months the United States air force has been bombing targets in Laos to the extent of some 100 strikes a day, I should like to ask the minister whether he is in possession of this information; and was he ever given the information by the United States government or by the Canadian representatives on the international control commission?

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Martin (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: LAOS-REPORTED BOMBINGS BY U.S. AIR FORCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my hon.
friend will recall that some weeks ago this question was asked and I indicated that the commission had received a complaint about these alleged bombings in Laos and that the commission, which of course includes a Canadian representative, depends upon those who made the complaint to facilitate the commission's examination of the allegations. Such permission has not yet been granted.

maintopic: LAOS-REPORTED BOMBINGS BY U.S. AIR FORCE
speechtext: May I ask a supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. Will any representations be made either to the government of Laos or the United States government for permission to investigate these charges?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: LAOS-REPORTED BOMBINGS BY U.S. AIR FORCE
speechtext: The permission in :his case in practical terms would not necessarily be given entirely by the royal government of Laos but also by those forces in Laos opposed militarily to the royal government. It is to these forces that a request by the Laos government to make an investigation must be made. The royal government of Laos does not fully control the whole territory of Laos.

maintopic: LAOS-REPORTED BOMBINGS BY U.S. AIR FORCE
speechtext: I have another supplementary question. With reference to the United States airports in Laos and in Thailand from which some of this bombing is going on, has any request been made of the government controlling these areas with regard to an investigation?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: LAOS-REPORTED BOMBINGS BY U.S. AIR FORCE
speechtext: There have been communications quite recently-I am not familiar with the details-addressed by the commission along the lines of those referred to by my hon. friend.

speechtext:
that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to authorize the payment of contributions by Canada toward the cost of insured medical care services incurred by provinces pursuant to provincial medical care insurance plans.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Batten in the chair.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare; Minister of Amateur Sport
subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OF CONTRIBUTIONS TOWARD COST OF INSURED MEDICAL CARE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, it is a privilege for me to sponsor this resolution and to begin debate on a program which, if approved, will enable the government of Canada to provide financial support to provincially administered medical care plans.
I would point out that this program is the fourth major step in the health insurance plan initiated some years ago by my colleague who now holds the position of Secretary of State for External Affairs. The other three are the health grants program, hospital insurance, and the establishment of the health resources fund.
In 1948, when the health grants were being discussed in this house, the then prime minister described them as being fundamental prerequisites of a nation-wide system of health insurance. The second phase, which was also piloted by my colleague now the Secretary of State for External Affairs through the legislative procedures in the spring of 1957, culminated in the hospital insurance program which provides benefits to virtually the whole population of our country. Members, of course will be familiar with the health resources fund, which was only recently approved by this parliament.
I am proud, Mr. Chairman, to be the pilot of this new measure, which will extend the benefits now available beyond the doors of the hospital, ensuring the availability of physicians' services whether these be provided in the doctor's office or in the patient's home. As hon. members know, the federal government has for some years been examining ways and means of ensuring that the opportunity for good health which is now viewed in western democracies as a right possessed by all should be available to every citizen of our country.
This effort springs not only from a deepening of our humanitarian concern for our fellow citizens, but from a realization that we
July 12, 1966

cannot afford the social and economic consequences of our failure to do so. In an industrial country such as ours we cannot afford the loss to our economy stemming from ill health.
It was these considerations, undoubtedly, which led to the appointment of the royal commission on health services, whose report has been subjected to considerable study by the government. The royal commission on health services, consisting as it did of representative professional personnel, recruited a corp of experts in many health fields and had the assistance of many of the best brains in Canada, to quote the chairman, an eminent Canadian jurist. It was the view of the royal commission on health services that there is an enormous gap between our scientific knowledge and skills on the one hand and our organizational and financial arrangements to apply them to the needs of men, on the other.
The commission described its recommendations as a method of closing this gap. One of its recommendations was partially implemented by the Health Resources Fund Act recently passed by the house. Another essential recommendation was for a comprehensive universal health services program consisting of several phases, one of which is for a universal program of medical services benefits-

These are the fundamental points which I believe every Canadian can and does support. The question is how best we can assure that this goal is met. The federal government's proposal, as hon. members know, is to offer the provinces a sizeable sum of money to support provincial medical care insurance programs which meet certain established standards.

July 12, 1966
Health and Welfare
We have taken this approach because we recognized that under our constitution health is a provincial responsibility and, because of this, federal initiative in this field is limited to encouraging provincial action. This is an important point, but one which I am afraid has been lost sight of in some of the debates on this subject.
It would be much simpler and, to some, more attractive to shunt these considerations aside and promise broad and direct federal action in this field. But in practice this would amount to little more than an exercise in futility, for it would mean making federal promises that are not within the federal power to keep.
It may be a matter of interest to members to note the manner in which changing times and conditions are reflected in the varying methods by which federal assistance has been made to provincial programs in the unfolding of our health insurance plan. When the health grants were introduced in 1948, many provincial governments were financially hard-pressed and because of this condition, but at the same time respecting the constitutional position, the federal government set up a series of health grants only some of which required the matching of the funds by a province. Thus, for many years in certain areas, the federal government has been providing through some of the health grants payments in full for projects designed and administered by the provincial governments.
By the time the hospital insurance program was introduced, federal sharing had become the usual means through which the government of Canada made contributions toward programs which clearly fell within provincial jurisdiction. Thus, the hospital insurance program became a conditional grants program under which the federal government began providing very considerable sums of money, but only with respect to shareable items of expenditure approved by the provincial governments.
The present phase of health insurance comes at a time when the conditional grants technique is undergoing some rethinking. Hence, it would not be in conformity with this policy to bring in a measure designed along the lines of existing conditional grant programs.

speechtext:
The resolution under consideration does not envisage a plan designed along the lines of existing grant programs but employs another avenue through which federal support will be provided. I shall discuss this further later in my remarks.
I have mentioned that there is no question at this time as to the role allocated to the provinces under our constitution in the health field. This role is a predominant one, and provincial governments individually will devise programs, as some have in fact already done, which undoubtedly will differ from province to province, as existing programs already do.
At the same time not all of the provinces have the same fiscal capability of providing such programs or of meeting the costs of programs designed for all residents. Thus, although Canada is one country a Canadian resident of one province may be at a distinct disadvantage when compared with a Canadian resident of another province.
Of even greater national concern is the disadvantage which may be suffered by a Canadian who, having resided in one province, moves to another province only to find that his position is the same as it might have
July 12, 1966

been had he moved to a point beyond his own national boundaries. Clearly these are considerations which give rise to certain federal responsibilities in the health and welfare fields.
Thus while it is the policy of this government to redefine its role in so far as conditional grant programs are concerned, it may not abrogate its obligation to ensure the national character of our country by establishing an acceptable level of services available to all citizens. It is proposed, therefore, that with the full co-operation of the provinces the federal government will support medical care programs which meet the four basic principles which the government of Canada believes will serve the national interest.
The first of these principles involves the scope of benefits which it is considered should be made available as a minimum, regardless of any other benefits a province may wish to include as well. It is considered that the medical care program should offer all of the services provided by physicians.
This would mean that the services of general practitioners and specialists would be insured services, regardless of where these services were made available. Whether the insured person is seen by the physician in the doctor's office, in the hospital, in a nursing home, or in a private home belonging to the insured person or to anyone else, the benefits of the medical care plan should be available.
Provincial governments, may of course, wish to expand the provincial programs so as to include additional benefits; there is nothing in the federal plan to deter them from doing so. We have assured the provincial governments that as soon as there is a consensus on the timing of further benefits to be provided over and above physicians' services, the federal government would consider enlarging appropriately and in due course the scope of benefits to which it would be prepared to contribute. As a first phase, however, the present resolution contemplates only the provision of physicians' services.
The second principle which is considered to be essential if the federal government is to make substantial financial contributions is that of coverage. In discussions with the provinces the matter of universal coverage, which we feel to be essential, has been examined carefully and closely. We have explained to the provinces that the principle of universal coverage should not be confused with compulsory coverage.
Health and Welfare
It is a fact that if a province chooses to finance its share of the costs by levying a premium, then and only then would the question of compulsion arise. It would be the decision of a province whether premiums would be compulsory in the sense that taxes are compulsory. Certainly this measure does not contemplate compulsion on individual doctors to join a plan; nor would there be any compulsion on individual persons to use the services provided under the plan.
I do not wish to appear to be splitting hairs, but it would seem to me that certain adverse comments which have been made on the question of compulsion give the impression that doctors would be required to treat patients they do not wish to treat and that individuals would be required to accept benefits under a program which they did not wish to accept. At the risk of repeating myself on this point, I should like categorically to state that neither of these two circumstances would be involved in the principle of universal coverage in the context of medical care.

Members might be interested in an assessment of the experience which has been gained in this regard under the various provincial hospital insurance plans. It will be recalled that under that program insured services were also required to be made available on equal terms and conditions to all residents. Universal coverage was automatically achieved in those provinces which chose to finance their share of the costs out of the general revenues of the province, or by means of a sales tax, or by a combination of these methods with or without an authorized charge for which provision was made in the legislation.

This entailed the registration of individuals and the payment of the premium fixed by provincial legislation. Nevertheless, the extent of coverage under hospital insurance at the present time in all provinces, including the province with a partial voluntary element, is now over 99 per cent of the eligible population.
I have explained this situation in some detail because I am anxious to illustrate my initial point, that universal coverage does not necessarily mean compulsory coverage.
In my discussions with the provinces as to what percentage of coverage the federal government will be prepared to view as universal, if a premium system of financing were adopted, I have agreed that for the initial period coverage of 90 per cent would be acceptable. It would be expected, of course, that this would rise to 95 per cent over a period of time.
Hon. members may ask why the federal government considers the principle of universal coverage to be so important. I believe that if the considerable expenditures which will have to be made to provincial programs are to be justified, then the federal government must have the assurance that as many people as possible will benefit. That is the case for the federal parliament. From the national point of view it is also essential to ensure that there is no differentiation in coverage between the residents of one province and another if federal funds are to be provided.
Before I leave the question of universal coverage I should like to draw the attention of hon. members to the report of the Royal Commission on Health Services and to studies made for that commission. All of these reached the same conclusion on the need for universality.
The third principle which the federal government considers to be essential is that of public administration. It is obvious that when the federal government makes substantial financial contributions available to the provinces, a provincial government must be capable of taking full responsibility for the use to which these contributions are put. The provincial plans should be non-profit and subjected to public audit, and the administrators

of the plan should be answerable to the public through the provincial legislature.
Once more I would like to point to the experience we have had in hospital insurance, which is as relevant to public administration as to universal coverage. Hospital insurance programs, without exception, are administered by the provincial governments, either directly by departments of health or, alternatively, by commissions established by provincial governments specifically for this purpose. I believe I am correct in saying that there is no jurisdiction in this country which has had reason to regret this method of administration.
The last principle which it is considered essential to incorporate in provincial medical care plans relates to transferability or, if you like, portability. This simply means that when a resident of one province moves to another province his entitlement to benefits will continue long enough for him to become entitled to benefits in the new province.

Insured services, of course, mean medically necessary services provided by medical practitioners. If such a program were to be provided in all provinces next year, it is estimated that the cost to the federal treasury for a full year would be $340 million.

It has been estimated that approximately $600 million would be spent next year on physicians' services if no change were made in the present methods of providing these services. I would ask hon. members, therefore, to compare the estimates on which we are basing public expenditures for public programs covering the whole population if these go into effect next year, namely, a total of $680 million including the provincial share of half the costs. Thus, by redistributing the estimated $600 million and adding another $80 million, all residents of all the provinces of Canada will have physicians' services available to them. These are estimates and these comments are for illustration purposes.
Members of the committee may be interested in knowing that some 6 million Canadians still lack any medical insurance coverage, and 3 million more have only limited coverage. Probably not more than 10 million Canadians at the present time have what could be called adequate comprehensive coverage. Those without adequate coverage include primarily residents of rural areas and people with moderate or low incomes, unable to acquire low-cost group insurance. I might mention that these figures do not include those who will benefit from the health provisions set out in the Canada Assistance Plan.
These, then, and the financial proposal are the principles which have been discussed with the provinces. The response from the provinces has, I must say, been most encouraging. Some provinces have already indicated their readiness to proceed by our target date of July 1, 1967. Others have not been in a position to commit themselves, although some of these pointed out that they would be able to change existing plans to meet the principles described above. I should like to state that no province has stated that it will definitely not participate although, as hon. members are undoubtedly aware, the premier of Alberta has expressed criticism of the proposal.

This would be a most appropriate way to mark our birthday, since it would ensure ready access to medical

care to all of our people, regardless of means, of pre-existing conditions, of age, or other circumstances which may have barred such access in the past.
At some time in each of our lives such care is necessary, if only to avoid the pitfalls of ill health. An investment in health is an investment in human resources. Only strong human resources can fulfil the promise offered to us by the other resources of our great country.

This situation concerns me a great deal because it is quite obvious that Canadian doctors are already carrying a 25 to 35 per cent greater work load than their counterparts in the United States and New Zealand. My one concern in raising this matter at the resolution stage is: How will we correct this shortage? The Hall Commission report said that we had to add 476 students each year to our present classes. Mr. Chairman, do you realize that this was said in 1964, two years ago? Do you realize that at that time the target date was 1971? This is the equivalent of nine or ten medical schools the size of Queen's University or Western. What is the cost? The nearest I can come to the cost is that Toronto university will add 75 this year to its freshmen year class and they say it will cost them $35 million to do this. There is $250 million right there. By 1970, 7,100 doctors must be added to the profession. This means that we must have 11,860 doctors by that time, so that you have 5,340 left as a minimum after taking out retirements, etc. We are in the same position with regard to dentists and nurses; 35,000 nurses have to be trained and some must receive university training. The Hall Commission report stated that there will be no substantial increase in graduating classes in medicine before 1971.
No move has been made until just recently, and this is 1966. I criticize the government for their lack of action in this regard, and I probably would be right in criticizing some of the universities as they are letting the public down. This report was made in 1964 and the target date was 1971, because it takes seven years to graduate a doctor with the minimal amount of training. It takes 11 years to train a specialist; and if a doctor is to have good, sound training he should spend two years as an intern, so there you have eight years for general practice.

This resolution should be taken step by step so that the plan does not break down completely and so that the minister will have a monument to what he has done rather than something that people will look at and say it is a great pillar of salt. I am really concerned about this situation, which is all the more serious because today in Canada out of every two doctors that graduate one carries on to be a specialist. In this country today 37 per cent of the doctors are certified specialists and 13 per cent are non-certified specialists.
In other words, Mr. Chairman, half the doctors that graduate today specialize, with more crowding into certain fields. We are short of optometrists. There has been a 75 per cent increase in the population but only a 15 per cent increase in optometrists. It takes seven years for a doctor to graduate, and here we are just starting in the fall of 1966. This means it will be 1976 before we will have doctors who have graduated with specialist training, and 1974 for General Practitioners.
There is another problem in this connection, namely, that four of our medical schools now are below par. Four have not enough good teachers or facilities to teach their students properly. I should like to read another article. Somebody might ask where it came from so I will make sure the source is on the record. It is a newspaper article which quotes the Canadian Medical Association Journal. The article says:
It has been whispered about for a long time. Now it is in the open: one-third of Canada's medical schools, during the last ten years, have been warned that if they don't improve they may lose their North American accreditation. This is a recognized method for judging the quality of medical schools, and loss of accreditation is a sad, bad blow . . .
"The primary fault in the four schools was not with respect to their basic orientation or the quality of existing staff, but rather that they had insufficient staff and resources to meet the needs of modern medicine."
How derelict in our duty can we be?
"If the teachers for the expansion of existing schools and the staffing of new medical schools are recruited from within Canada, a sort of academic musical chairs will occur in which the staffs of existing schools will be rapidly diluted, and, if the bidding is brisk, an unfortunate concentration of the best talent in a few centres may develop."
And it surely will be through lack of facilities.
The editorial is an urgent appeal for government to heed the warnings and the proposals of the Gundy report on medical education. It refers to the "twilight sleep of lethargy" which enfolds both the public and those in high places. It does not add- although we gladly do-that a government that has
Health and Welfare
pushed its expenditures beyond the $9 billion mark, should find it possible to rectify and reverse the existing starvation of medical science.
This brings me to another point. We are spending $10 million on research. The United States is spending $1,200 million. We have been very derelict in this chamber in this regard. If this medicare plan breaks down and is not handled most carefully a step at a time, there will surely be serious consequences because we have not the background at present to operate such a plan. And who is responsible? This government in particular and other governments are responsible because of their starvation of medical science and education. The article continues:
Canadians complain endlessly about their abject position vis-a-vis the United States. But they refuse to face the fact that much of it is simply due to failure to spend money where it will do the most good. We are prepared, apparently, to institute medicare at vast expense. We do little to improve medical science and education upon which, obviously, medicare ultimately depends. The amount of money involved is trifling in comparison to the global budget total.
What are we going to do about this situation? Whether we have medicare does not matter so much. The important thing is the care of those people who need medical attention. These are the people we must protect, because we are not providing this medical care at the moment. How are we to get out of this rut? I have already said that we are extremely short of teachers, so short, in fact, that four universities may lose their accreditation. How do we get these teachers? Do we train our graduates in Canada or do we bring back some of our teacher scientists from the United States? We have supplied the United States with 200 to 400 medical graduates a year. The United States can count on well over 200 young, energetic Canadian doctors with 40 years of earning power, and this is costing this country a total earning power of over $100 million a year.

I will not take up much more time, Mr. Chairman. There are just a few more facts I wish to present. Only 2 per cent of our medical graduates will become teachers and only 0.5 per cent will become scientific researchers. This means we will have to get the teachers from somewhere if we are to man our medical schools and if we are to follow the recommendations of the Hall Commission. First we must train students, then doctors, then teachers and finally scientists.
Let me say, Mr. Chairman, that building palaces with fine laboratories is of no value if we do not have teachers, teacher scientists and pure scientists. For the past 15 years one-third of our doctors per year have been coming from Great Britain. In one year up to

600 doctors came from Great Britain. I knew the figure was high but I was amazed to see how high it was. I think it was in the year 1964 that three-quarters of all the graduates of British universities emigrated, and today 50 per cent of the interns in some of their, hospitals come from outside of Great Britain. A great many of them come from Africa and Asia.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare; Minister of Amateur Sport
subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OF CONTRIBUTIONS TOWARD COST OF INSURED MEDICAL CARE
speechtext: Will the hon. member permit a question? Why does he think the British doctors are coming to Canada and Canadian doctors are going to the U.S.? Has he any over-all explanation for this movement on the part of the members of the medical profession?

subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OF CONTRIBUTIONS TOWARD COST OF INSURED MEDICAL CARE
speechtext: I think the reasons for the movement of these doctors are better working conditions and the incentive of better pay. If the minister would look at the records he would find out that the average doctor in England looks after approximately 2,000 patients. I had the privilege of visiting the office of one of those doctors. There were chairs lined up along the walls of his office with many patients waiting. There must have been 20 or 25 people in that room. That doctor could not have possibly spent more than two or three minutes with each patient.

subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OF CONTRIBUTIONS TOWARD COST OF INSURED MEDICAL CARE
speechtext: Was that under the medical plan in England?

subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OF CONTRIBUTIONS TOWARD COST OF INSURED MEDICAL CARE
speechtext:
That was a few years back under the national health plan. In Orillia, whence I come, there are three doctors from Great Britain. Two are surgeons and one is a general practitioner. They have told me very definitely that their reason for leaving England was overwork and the fact that they were being regimented under politics. One doctor, whom I referred to earlier, was a very nice chap and he told me that he was being over-worked, as anybody with a work load of 2,000 or more patients must be.
The afternoon I saw him he referred one or two of his patients to the local hospital but he did not know when they would be admitted. He said it might be in two or three months time. I pointed out to him that one of his patients might be in a serious condition. He told me he had seen him on three or four previous occasions but the patient had not improved with the treatment that had been given him. The doctor did not follow his patient to the hospital. He was sent to an entirely new doctor who had never seen him
July 12. 1966



before and might not care to perform the surgery. This is the reason for the dissatisfaction of the doctors. To return to the case of this patient, he might, three months following his dismissal from the hospital, return to the doctor for a check-up but the doctor might not even have his history because of lack of time and facilities.
The immigration of foreign doctors has developed in us a lazy attitude in the last 15 years. We have been derelict in our duty to the Canadian people and the government has been derelict in its duty. I want to put that on the record.
[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare; Minister of Amateur Sport
subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OF CONTRIBUTIONS TOWARD COST OF INSURED MEDICAL CARE
speechtext: My hon. friend is suggesting that it is costing the Canadian society $50,000 a year to train a doctor and $100,000 to train a teacher or scientist. What is his conclusion from the movement of Canadian doctors to the United States, a movement which is quite unrelated to the medical care program we are now discussing? What steps should we take aside from medical care, which is quite unrelated?

I assume the minister did not hear me. What I said was that there should be an incentive given to these people to remain in Canada. It could be a research work or tax incentive for a few years. Doctors in the United States pay less taxes and get more salary, than doctors do here. I guess the minister missed that part of my speech, but I do believe I alluded to it. If I did not, I intended to.
I should like to refer to what Dr. T. W. Gorman, former President of the Nova Scotia Medical Society, said with respect to this problem. He comes from the minister's own area and he said the problem was serious. He recommended that the length of the medical course be reduced. He pointed out that the profession and the medical schools had a responsibility to supply quantity and quality and suggested a shorter medical course. Dr. Gorman suggested that area of eastern Canada was going to be very short of doctors. The minister must be well aware of these facts. We are short of trained doctors, short of teachers and scientists. The Hall Commission recognized there would be such a shortage up to 1971, but now that we are implementing a health plan the shortage will be accentuated by 1971. The minister has had ample time to introduce this plan; yet we are about two years behind schedule. I should like
Health and Welfare
to quote from page 14, volume I of the Hall Commission report:
We recognize, of course, that this whole program cannot be put into effect immediately or simultaneously in all provinces. We do not foresee the program coming forth full-grown but rather as an orderly and well planned series of steps which taken together will in a period of years accomplish our objective.

speechtext: The hon. member is not concluding that there is any contradiction between the conclusions of the Hall Commission and the proposal we are making today? What we are doing is completely compatible with their recommendations.

speechtext: If I understood the minister correctly he intimated that this plan would be effective across Canada. I realize he probably has to consider the wishes of the provinces, but he was estimating this plan would cover 90 per cent of the people. If I am wrong, I want to be corrected. All I can say is that the Hall Commission made its report in 1964 and we are now in 1966. At any rate, medical care will be available. Medical care is available in the province of Ontario and, as I have said, four million people are covered in that province. I should like to congratulate the Ontario Minister of Health for introducing OMSIP because it is a step in the right direction.
As I said a moment ago, I am reserving my decision on this plan until I see the bill. I am wondering if this is the type of step we should be taking. In the province of Ontario we have blind people's allowances, disabled persons' allowances, mothers' allowances, old age assistance, the rehabilitation act, and so on. There is assistance to those on lower incomes. If a family of two have a taxable income of $100 or less, the government pays 50 per cent of their medical expenses. Perhaps this is a better type of plan. I do not know. I noticed that in the last election campaign the present Minister of Trade and Commerce stated on November 4 that the

July 12, 1966
Health and Welfare
Liberal party may have to delay the introduction of a national medicare scheme because of the shortage of doctors and nurses. I am having similar thoughts. We may break down the whole system, and this is what worries me.
I noticed an alarming article in Barron's of England the other day under the heading, "Cradle to Grave?". The article indicated the British were turning away from socialized medicine. I hope we can avoid the pitfalls that have been evident in the British scheme. The British people have received reasonable care, but there have been many quarrels with doctors and complaints from patients. I am told that in England there are insurance companies that are now insuring people so they can get proper medical care. They would rather be under the care of their family doctor than be pushed around under the national health plan. These are the things I want to see avoided in Canada. I am greatly interested in making sure that we avoid these mistakes. I am sure the minister will feel this plan has to be as nearly right as we can make it. It is human to err, but I hope he will review the whole situation in consultation with the provincial ministers who know the situation in the provinces. I hope the minister will then come to the conclusion that he will proceed cautiously and carefully in light of what the ministers of health advise.
We should remember that today the Canadian people are getting fed up with taxes. They are paying more taxes than ever to the federal government, provincial governments and municipal governments. They are getting fed up, and they do not want any mistakes made in this plan. The reason we are having so many strikes and so much labour trouble is that the people do not have enough money to make ends meet. I say with great sincerity that I am not going to be unduly critical. I hope my criticism has been constructive. I should like to see a plan adopted that will be the best in the world. The minister nods his head but I am not sure, after listening to what he had to say, that he knows what the right thing is. I hope he is right because, personally, I like the minister. We owe it to the Canadian people to see that they get the best type of service possible so that we will make this country great medically. Then we will not lose graduates to the United States but will attract them to remain in Canada and we could have one of the greatest medical centres in the world for post-graduate work.

speechtext:
The Minister of National Health and Welfare was quite right, Mr. Chairman, when he said this is a historic day because it marks another milestone in Canada's long march toward comprehensive health insurance. The legislation which we hope will immediately follow this resolution will be another step in the attainment of a goal for which the Canadian people have been waiting a long time. I do not need to remind members of the day when the first official promise of comprehensive health insurance in Canada appeared in the Liberal party's platform at the convention in August of 1919.
The next time official notice was taken of this question by a Liberal government was in 1945 at the federal-provincial conference on reconstruction when the green book proposals set out a fully delineated health insurance program to be brought into operation in conjunction with the provinces. The other day I came across a copy of the Toronto Star for Wednesday, April 21, 1948, with the great, streamer headline, "Health Insurance At Once Said Plan Of Premier King".
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
In 1948 the people were led to believe that they were to have health insurance. The health grants of 1948 of course were of some assistance. The first real step was taken when legislation was brought down by the Liberal government in 1957 to set up national hospital insurance. Unfortunately that legislation was so restrictive that it was of no benefit to any province unless the majority of the provinces representing the majority of the people of Canada signified their intentions of coming into the plan. Consequently the plan was not established until a Conservative administration removed the restrictive features, and the hospital insurance plan became a reality in 1958.
Then we had the Hall Commission which did a superb piece of work and brought down in June of 1964 what I think is the finest statement on medicare that has ever been published in the English language. That commission recommended immediate action. It asked that within six months of the report being tabled the government convene a federal-provincial conference. The government did convene a conference here in Ottawa on July 19 and 20 of 1965. And on this day, July 12, 1966, we have a resolution preceding the bill which will take the next step in comprehensive health insurance, namely, a measure to provide for medical care for all Canadians in
July 12, 1966

those provinces where the provincial governments are prepared to co-operate in setting up such a plan.
Before I comment on this program may I say I think we should keep in mind that it is only a step in a long-term program, that even though medical care is being established I think we have been too long in getting to it, and that the plan still leaves a large area of health needs untouched. We shall still have to think in terms of essential and prescribed drugs, dental care, optometric care, and all of the ancillary health services. We must bear in mind that, while the present measure is one of the most important steps, we must be under no illusion that the implementation of the plan to be contained in the legislation coming before us is the end of the road.
I want to commend the minister for the work he has done and which his predecessor did in this field. I am sure that they will get a good deal of criticism from many quarters about the drain on the federal treasury and about the increased costs which can be anticipated. I think the public sometimes lose sight of the fact which the minister pointed out this afternoon, that it is already costing the Canadian people some $600,000 a year for this kind of care and that the cost of medicare is not a new cost. It is simply a redistribution of the cost, so that instead of the burden being placed on the sick, it is distributed over the entire population on a basis that has some relation to ability to pay.

The hon. member says:
"What about the taxes?" Well, what about paying doctors' bills? People who pay taxes also pay doctors' bills. Most of us would rather pay taxes when we are well than pay doctors' bills when we are sick.

speechtext:
The hon. member for Simcoe East made some reference to the fact that in Saskatchewan our experience with hospital insurance was that the load went up some 26 per cent. This is true. It levelled out, however, once we got over the backlog. I do not think that medicare will go up at the same rate; which might be of some comfort to the minister.
Perhaps I could draw his attention to the experience of Saskatchewan. The Thompson committee, which did a great deal of research into this matter before the legislation was introduced in 1961, gave it as their opinion 23033-4781
Health and Welfare
that the plan would probably cost about $25 million annually and that the cost would rise for a while and then level off. The interesting thing is that the plan, which is now in its fourth year, never reached $25 million and in fact has slightly declined lately.
An article that appeared in the Edmonton Bulletin on June 15, 1966, had this to say:
A leader of the 1962 Saskatchewan doctors' strike admitted Tuesday some of his profession's fears about medicare have proved unfounded . . .
Dr. Barootes broke what he called a self-imposed vow of silence. He told his colleagues:-
This was at the Canadian Medical Association Conference:
"Some of the qualms we have had have been disproved and some of us should revise our thinking. The idea that total medical care results in constantly-mounting costs has been shattered," he
said.
The fact is, he said, that the total cost of Saskatchewan medicare dropped last year by $500,000, from $23 million to $22.5 million . . .
He said in an interview later he could not explain why medicare costs have not shot up, as he and other doctors had predicted. He said it may be because Saskatchewan residents have been saturated with medical service-that they now have been treated for all the ailments that, before medicare, went untreated.
This is a courageous statement by Dr. E.W. Barootes, who was chairman of the committee that masterminded the doctors' strike in Saskatchewan. He is a man for whom I have great respect. While I cannot agree with him, I think he is the kind of man who, when he found out that he was wrong, was quite willing to admit that his estimates of the fantastic costs which medicare was supposed to impose upon the people were not well-founded.
Since we have very limited time at this stage of debate I shall confine myself to two questions. One is, what kind of medicare plan are we to get, and the second is, when are we to get it? I am convinced that there is little value in setting up a medicare plan unless it is soundly based. It would be better to postpone the plan than to have a poorly structured plan because once the plan is launched it will take years to undo the damage if it is not soundly based. It is extremely important, therefore, that this plan be on a sound basis.
That sound basis, of course, has been spelled out by the Hall Commission in its very excellent report. It was also spelled out by the Prime Minister in the four basic principles which he set forth as the criteria upon which the medicare plan should be based. I am hopeful that when the legislation

July 12, 1966
Health and Welfare
is brought down it will be on all fours with the criteria elucidated by the Prime Minister on July 19 and 20 of last year. These four criteria have already been mentioned by the minister.
The Prime Minister in his address to the federal-provincial conference said that the first principle was that the scope of benefits should be, broadly speaking, all the services provided by physicians, both general practitioners and specialists. He went on to say:
A complete health plan would include dental treatment, prescribed drugs, and other important services, and there is nothing in the approach we propose to prevent these being included, from the start or later, if this were the general wish.
He also said:
We regard comprehensive physicians' services as the initial minimum.
In light of that statement about the scope of benefits I was hoping that the measure which the minister was going to bring down would be an open-ended plan that would allow the provinces to proceed as fast as they were ready to do so, and that the plan would not slow the provinces down to the pace of the slowest of the Canadian family.
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
I noticed that the minister in his statement this afternoon said, if I may quote him, "We have assured the provincial governments that as soon as there is a consensus on the timing of further benefits to be provided over and above physicians' services, the federal government would consider enlarging appropriately, and in due course, the scope of benefits to which it would be prepared to contribute."
I wish to ask the minister why we should have to wait for a consensus. I am certain that had we waited for a consensus in 1957 and 1958 the hospital insurance plan would have been long delayed. I see no reason why this legislation should not be sufficiently flexible to provide that when a province has established physicians' care under the plan- and one province has already done so-it is free to make provision for some other health service. This would be in accordance with the green book proposals of 1945.
The province would have a choice. It could select dental care and might start with dental care for children. It could select optometric care or the provision of certain drugs such as insulin and cortisone, and then move into the field of prescribed drugs. I had hoped for legislation sufficiently flexible to make it possible for a province to move as fast as it could build the necessary administration and

find the funds with which to pay its share of the cost.
I am disappointed that the scope of the benefits is to be restricted entirely to physicians services and that the program will not be sufficiently flexible to enable other health benefits to be added as provinces are prepared to make them available. I hope the minister will reconsider this matter and that he will not ask the provinces which are most anxious to proceed to wait for a consensus. This is an attractive modern term which everybody likes to use nowadays. But I think we should be encouraging the provinces which wish to move ahead, not asking them to wait until the more laggard provinces are prepared to catch up with them.
The second principle which the Prime Minister laid down in his address to the federal-provincial conference on July 19 was as follows:
Second, we would propose that the plan should be universal. That is to say, it should cover all residents in the province on uniform terms and conditions.
The next day, July 20, the Prime Minister spelled out in more detail those basic conditions, and on this matter of universality he said:
The objective, as we see it, must be universal coverage. I cannot see any basis otherwise for a federal contribution.
He went on to say:
There is often confusion as to the relation between universality and compulsion. Our purpose is that everyone should qualify for benefits. This involves compulsion in the sense that, if a premium is chosen by a province as part of the method of financing, the premium would be compulsory in the sense that taxes are compulsory. Obviously there is no compulsion on people to use the services, nor any compulsion on the individual doctor to join the plan if the demand for his services is such that he can practice successfully outside it.
He went on to say:
The "principle of need" which was referred to yesterday rejects the idea of universality on the grounds that, if low-income people are covered, others can afford the premiums under private insurance plans. To us, the weaknesses of this are that (1) it sets up an undesirable distinction according to income levels; and (2) even people with quite high incomes can face medical costs which are just as crippling as ordinary illnesses are for low-income people. Most such people may be covered by private plans, but not all will be. In practice, therefore, no extension of private plans will meet all the needs.
I have put this on record, Mr. Chairman, because I think these words of the Prime Minister should be kept in mind when we come to examining the legislation and the
July 12, 1966

extent to which the general principles laid down are, in fact, implemented in the statute itself.
The third principle which the Prime Minister enunciated at the federal-provincial conference is as follows:
Third, I think it will readily be agreed that a federal contribution can properly be made available only to a plan which is publicly administered, either directly by the provincial government or by a provincial non-profit agency.
Elaborating on this the next day, the Prime Minister said:
A universal plan with a federal contribution must be a plan for which the provincial government takes full responsibility. It is necessarily a replacement of existing plans of other types. The procedures followed by provincial governments in dealing with the transitional arrangements in the case of hospital insurance would seem to have been highly satisfactory and equally applicable in the case of medical Insurance. This means that the experience and skills involved in carrying out existing large programs can be transferred to the public program.
Again, as in the case of hospital insurance, there will of course be scope for the continuation of private insurance for services above those provided in the public plan.
I underline the word "above"-not as part of the public plan.

The final point which the Prime Minister outlined in his speech of July 19 was as follows:
-and finally, I think it is important to recognize the mobility of Canadians; each provincial plan should therefore provide full transferability of benefits when people are absent from the province or when they move their homes to another province.
Of course there will be no quarrel with that. That is basic.
In answer to the question put by the hon. member for Macleod, who was worried about what happens when people go overseas, under the medicare plan in Saskatchewan-and I assume most provinces will follow the same practice-the medicare card is acceptable in any country of the world for medical services provided in another country. The bill can either be sent to the Saskatchewan medicare commission or the patient can pay the bill himself and later get reimbursement from the commission.
May I now turn briefly to the other question which is, when will we get medicare? The government has talked about a target date of July 1, 1967, but I have been somewhat concerned about the statement made by the Minister of Finance last November 5 when he said medicare would probably have to be postponed because of the shortage of doctors. I hope the government will not delay.
There is much in what the hon. member for Simcoe East has said about the need for more doctors, the need for medical schools and the need for more medical research. Also he is quite correct when he says that we, the Canadian people, have been derelict for the last 20 years in grappling with this problem. But on the other hand I want to say to the minister that if we delay in setting up medicare until the situation is entirely satisfactory, the plan will never be put into operation.
There is something about human nature whereby we never do things until we have to do them. We work best in a crisis and under pressure, and since the preparatory work has not been done-there has been some done but not sufficient-I would hope the government would go ahead with medicare and that it would cling to its target date of July 1, 1967.
The hon. member for Simcoe East warned the government not to fall into the pitfalls experienced in Great Britain. I think he was

somewhat unfair to the British health plan when he spoke about a doctor sending patients to hospitals where some other doctor treated them. That has been the practice in Britain, Germany and other western European countries for a century. They have a totally different medical system. They separate their doctors into physicians and surgeons, and a general practitioner is not allowed to take his patient into a hospital.
The things to which my hon. friend has referred cannot be attributed to the British health plan. If one wants to use quotations, I can say that one day at a luncheon meeting I was addressing in London I sat beside one very senior Conservative cabinet minister who said to me, "I voted against the British health plan, I campaigned against it, but I have to admit now it is the best thing we have ever done on these islands. Even if it cost us twice what it is costing, it would be worth it; our children are healthier and our general level of health is vastly superior to anything it has ever been throughout our history."
Of course the hon. member for Simcoe East is right. There has been congestion. There have been problems and wrinkles to be ironed out, as there will be in the Canadian health plan, but if we wait until we have a perfect setup we will never start.
We in Canada have waited far too long for a step which has already been taken by most of the countries of western Europe, and in fact taken by some of them before the turn of the century. The information I want to get from the minister is whether the government is going to proceed with this legislation. We have had a variety of reports. As late as June 6 the house leader, the Minister of Public Works, said that the medicare bill would be dealt with before the summer recess. More recently he has been talking about only the resolution being passed.
Three times on Sunday the C.B.C. reported that the Prime Minister had indicated he wanted all stages of the medicare legislation passed before a summer recess. I do not know whether that is true. The C.B.C. is sometimes given to managing the news and lately has taken to manufacturing it. This also may have been manufactured, but I want to say to the government that it will make a great mistake if it does not deal with this legislation before we adjourn.
If this legislation is left until the fall some of the provinces may use that as an excuse to
July 12, 1966

say they have not had sufficient time to prepare the complementary legislation which they must submit to their legislatures. I think any province that is really interested could have its legislation drafted by now or would be in the process of drafting it, but the minister and this house cannot afford to give any province an alibi for not being ready to come into this plan on July 1 next.
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
I think this matter ought to be dealt with at this session before we recess for a summer adjournment. It may be said that members wish to get back to their constituencies. Certainly, as much as any other member, I would like to get back to my constituency. I may point out to the government that it is not our fault that this legislation was not brought down two or three months ago; it is not our fault that the government has dallied and delayed in bringing this matter to the attention of the house. But now that it is here I suggest we have a duty to the people of Canada and have a debt to posterity to see that this legislation is put on the statute books of Canada before we leave here for a summer holiday. I should like to tell the government that so far as members of this party are concerned we are prepared to stay here and take whatever time is necessary to deal with this legislation.
A while ago a question was asked with regard to whether this legislation would go to the committee on health and welfare. We would point out to the minister that this legislation is the result of a royal commission which spent four years studying this matter and travelling from one end of Canada to the other. In every section of Canada the people were allowed to make representations irrespective of who they were, what their profes-ion was or what their interest was. This matter has been amply studied. Moreover, this legislation is enabling legislation. The real details of the medicare program will be drafted by the provincial legislatures. All this parliament can do is, first, say that the government of Canada will pay half the average per capita cost of providing this service in any province which cares to establish a plan and, second, it can lay down the basic principles upon which that provincial plan must be predicated. This is all this parliament can do. I see no reason why those principles cannot be put into legislation without submitting this matter to a committee. If the provinces wish to submit their legislation to provincial committees to discuss the details of the plan, that is their business.
Health and Welfare
I do plead with the minister, and perhaps more necessarily with some of the other members of the government: Do not let this house adjourn for the summer recess without passing this legislation. I ask the government not to weaken and not to delay. I believe the members of this house are prepared to support the minister in passing this legislation as expeditiously as possible. All the members of this house are asking of the government is that they give us some leadership in this regard. If we get that leadership, we will give the government continued co-operation to see that this legislation is passed without delay. It is important legislation because, as the minister himself has already said, this is another milestone in Canada's march toward the day when every Canadian citizen will be entitled to health services irrespective of their colour, their race or their ability to pay. For that reason we want it placed on the statute books as quickly as possible.
