speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I listened very intently to the speech made by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Douglas) and I must say that I am at variance with him on several points, for instance, when he asks us to whisk this legislation through. The hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Douglas) says that it is not even necessary to refer this bill to a committee for consideration, while we do not even have the bill before us yet.
And everything seems simplified in the mind of the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam. Again this afternoon, during the question period, we asked if certain provinces which are a little more jealous of their constitutional rights want tax compensation instead of a subsidy. What would happen? Well, the minister seemed a little uncertain, and I am convinced that there is nothing in the bill now to cover that and that consideration in committee could be helpful in finding a solution to those problems.
The hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam seems eager to hurry things, and not give the members of the house or the provinces too much of an opportunity to consider this legislation. Yet, it must be recalled that health is a provincial matter, and that the provinces are the ones which, in the final analysis under the terms of the constitution, have jurisdiction in the field of health.

July 12. 1366
Health and Welfare
And that is why I am surprised at that last-minute suggestion made by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam. Although we are ready to sit during the summer, although we are ready to study Canadian problems, we are not ready to whisk such legislation through.
What we would be ready to accept, however, is that the bill be referred to the committee and that the committee sit during the summer months to take it under consideration. That would be acceptable to us.
We want to take our time in studying this bill, not because we want to avoid working, nor shirk our duty, but because, on the contrary, we want it looked into properly so that, later on, we will not blame ourselves.
The hon. member for Bumaby-Coquitlam mentioned, as if it were something terrible, that health insurance should not be in the hands of private enterprise, adding that it would then be more costly.
Mr. Chairman, I should like to point out that, in Canada, or at least in the province of Quebec, there are health insurance companies the purpose of which is not to make profit; they operate very well and give satisfaction to those who deal with them. For instance, the Quebec Health Service or Blue Cross can manage that type of health insurance program, at a lesser cost than what it would cost the state.
Saskatchewan has been given as an example. But it is in that province that the population has grown the least. Let someone tell us why the people of Saskatchewan leave it to go and live in Alberta and British Columbia. They do, because they are fed up with socialism, where the state tries to manage everything for the individual. The individual is not trusted; he is denied his responsibilities. And so, the citizens of Saskatchewan go elsewhere to live. The last census proved it. If there is a province where the population did not increase, that is Saskatchewan.
To what is that due? To the fact that an attempt was made to decrease the responsibilities of the individual, to strip him of his personality, in order to hand everything over to the state. We can see what it has led to: not much. It kept the province from progressing in comparison with the other prairie provinces which have developed much more rapidly.
Well, Mr. Chairman, I am not prepared to let this bill be rushed through in such a way
[Mr. Grcgoire l
that will prevent us from realizing what has happened. We do not even have a copy of the bill.
If the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam agrees to the committee sitting during the summer so that the hon. members can look into this bill, we have no objection. But if they try to railroad a bill in such a way that nobody is able to see anything, well, then we raise an objection.
Mr. Chairman, it was said a while ago that the federal government had only two things to do: to pay the 50 per cent of the cost and, second, to enumerate the conditions. But we should like to know how the 50 per cent will be paid to the provinces. We do not agree at all with the federal government collecting tax money and then saying to the provinces: set up a program in such a way so as to use this tax money in an orderly fashion. We prefer a system like the one adopted for many other programs, that is a fiscal compensation. If they expect that medicare is going to cost such an amount to the province of Quebec and the federal government is going to pay half the cost, the province of Quebec should get a fiscal equivalent for what that will cost the federal government.
That is one of the first conditions we would like to see included in the bill, because we believe it is very important that the jurisdiction of the provincial government in the field of health should be respected as much as possible. We think that is possible in the case of medicare. That has been done in other areas, in many joint programs; therefore, why could this not be done with medicare? I think the minister will not object and if he failed to make such provision in the bill, he will see to it, before introducing the bill, to move an amendment so as to enable the provinces to choose either between a fiscal compensation or any other plan that the federal government will make available to them or leave them free to accept.
As far as the province of Quebec is concerned, it is a known fact that this province has decided to establish its own medicare plan. The only thing we can do here to support this plan is to demand that a fiscal compensation rather than a straight subsidy or grant be paid by the federal government, because we feel that the federal government would override its jurisdiction and we are against any further infringements on the rights of the provinces. Once the federal government has decided to pay a certain amount
July 12. 1966

or give a fiscal compensation, it may then leave the provinces a free hand in the administration of their medicare plan.
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
If the provinces want to go through private, non-profit organizations, let them. In many cases, it has been demonstrated that the administration of such a plan by a private organization-by this I mean a private, non-profit insurance company-is preferable and less expensive. Let the provinces take their own decisions on their own programs, since this is under their jurisdiction, under their responsibility in this area of health.
Mr. Chairman, that is all we have to say at this stage and we object to this being a state plan, where all is controlled by the state, that is the doctors, the drugs, the hospitals and the rest. We want individuals to preserve their right to choose, that they may continue to live in accordance with their own decisions and their own responsibilities; we object to any infringement by the state in the field of health. The goal to be attained in a health insurance plan is to provide health care for all Canadians, regardless of wealth, rank, race, religion, or age. The objective is to make it possible for each citizen to have access to medical care. There is a way to reach that goal. It can be done through a government program administered, directed, supervised, inspected by the government, and we want none of that.
In the field of health, even more than in others, the individual has a right to his freedom, he must be free to choose his own plan, his own doctor. And in the field of health also, the doctors must be left free. Since medicine is a profession, we must leave to the doctors as much personal ambition as possible, as much personal initiative as possible; only if those conditions are respected will we have good doctors, in short competent doctors. They must not be turned into government employees. They must not be turned into bureaucrats who will have to work in shifts. We must give that profession all the freedom it needs. We must also give the individual, the human being, all the freedom he needs. The government must set up a plan where everyone will be free to choose but will have access to medical care, whatever his means, and even if he has no money at all, to get medical attention when he is sick, to go to the hospital when the need arises, to see a doctor.
Health and Welfare
That is the goal to be attained and the bill which will be introduced should seek to attain that goal, while leaving his freedom to the individual and the human being.
Mr. Chairman, the minister did not mention in his statement what such care will be; he said: it must be as general as possible. Well, it will be necessary to include all medical care, including dental care, etc.
Mr. Chairman, such are the few remarks we wanted to make; we will wait until we see the bill before discussing it further. We believe that it should be referred to the committee for further study. If that can be done during the summer months, we are ready to do it; if that must be postponed until the fall, we would deplore it, because we would prefer things to go even faster, but in any event, we are ready to co-operate if the bill is referred to the committee for further study, so that the legislation will be the best possible, to the benefit of each and every Canadian citizen.

subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OF CONTRIBUTIONS TOWARD COST OF INSURED MEDICAL CARE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in commenting on this resolution, which is a preliminary to the medicare legislation that has been talked about by the government now for such a long period of time, I should like to say that we in the Social Credit party are in complete agreement with the proposition advanced by the minister that every Canadian citizen and every Canadian family, regardless of financial status or any other classification that might be applied, must have full access to the highest quality, comprehensive health care possible, according to physical or mental needs. This is a basic principle, and I think we, not only as members of this house but as members of society as a whole, must assure every Canadian citizen and every Canadian family that it will be achieved.
In this regard I am just as anxious as any member of the New Democratic Party, the government or any other member of the house to see that every Canadian citizen receives complete health care according to his needs at a price he can afford. Therefore my remarks regarding this resolution at this time and in reply to the minister's statement are not in disagreement with that objective-we agree with that objective-but rather in disagreement with the method proposed as to how this objective should be achieved. Just because the government says that medicare is the most logical, efficient and economic way of achieving this objective, and just because

July 12, 1966
Health and Welfare
the government suggests that its proposal is the best way of achieving this objective, does not make this necessarily true.
Having said that, I do not believe that the federal, provincial or municipal governments have any responsibility to care for the health needs of Canadian citizens who are themselves able to provide that care. That is the false philosophy of the welfare state. In my opinion the government does have a responsibility to assist those who are unable to provide for their own needs. If we accomplish that then we are meeting our responsibilities as our brothers' keepers.
Nothing less than the very best of health care must be made available to all Canadian citizens according to their needs, but that does not mean the government must provide this care. I have in mind now those citizens who are able to provide for themselves. If we provide hospitals, health services and various forms of health treatment then I think it is only reasonable for everyone to have access to them, but to throw that whole responsibility on the shoulders of the government is not necessary; in fact, it is wrong.
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)
We are told today that this legislation is intended to pay for only physicians' services and the estimated cost is approximately $28 per capita, half of which is to be paid by the federal government. This represents only one small area of the over-all field of health care. For those who advance the thesis that the government is responsible for everyone, regardless of whether they can afford it or not, this is a major step. However, it is committing not only the federal government but the provincial governments to a program that will be vastly more expensive than $28 per capita. In fact, it is just the beginning, because if we say we are going to supply only physicians' services we are neglecting very important areas of health care that must later be included in the plan.
What about optometric care, particularly for our children? What about dental care? What about other forms of health care that are legitimate in the over-all field of caring for the sick, such as chiropractic treatment? These things must be included later. Therefore in dealing with this legislation we are actually committing ourselves to a program of health care that will be vastly more expensive than the plan we are talking about now.
I believe there are other things that are vitally important and which are inherent in this legislation. A government-dominated

scheme, whether it is compulsory by direct premium or compulsory by being charged to general taxation leads inevitably to a loss of individual freedom. Nothing is more compulsory than taxation. Is it not possible for us in this democratic society to meet our basic responsibility to our fellow men without destroying, weakening or eroding those basic elements of freedom that are inherent in the democratic process? I think it is. Therefore I think we in this house who represent the Canadian people should make sure that in approaching the objective with which we all must agree we are using the most efficient and effective methods. I do not believe the legislation as outlined in this resolution and the minister's statement is the most efficient and effective method. To say that we must deal with this matter prior to the recess is to cut short essential discussion on the one hand and on the other to force upon the provinces and the people of Canada something which cannot deal with that quickly. It has been said that the report of the Royal Commission on Health Services has adequately dealt with the problem. I disagree. It made recommendations, some of which are very excellent. But this may not be the best answer to the problem. Just to commit the government to this phase of health care is to override many of the recommendations that were made relating to the supplying of adequate services to meet the needs of our people as they relate to health care.
The first speaker after the minister in the debate this afternoon, the hon. member for Simcoe East, a man in the medical profession whom I respect very much, raised a point that was also included in the report of the Royal Commission on Health Services. I refer to our ability to provide the facilities, doctors and nurses necessary for the proper functioning of this program. Just to ignore certain aspects of the commission's report because we think we must now force a commitment upon the government of Canada and the governments of the provinces is absolutely wrong. In fact, Mr. Chairman, I am convinced that if the public were fully aware of the ultimate cost in relation to the benefits that will be received under the legislation as proposed at the present time, they would be most hesitant to accept such a plan; in fact, I think they would reject it.
Another vital area, as medical care relates to the general field of welfare, is that of priorities. I believe we are approaching the
July 12, 1966

general responsibility of public welfare in reverse. There are priorities within our responsibilities in the area of public welfare which must be established. We cannot afford, the public purse cannot pay for, the over-all cost of public welfare to which we are today committing ourselves.
I think the basic priority that we have to the public at large and to our children is one of education. I believe it is necessary to make sure that we give education the priority it must have. I refer not only to general education but to the education involved in giving our people the health care they deserve. This includes the training of doctors, the building of hospitals and providing research facilities. If we move in with a medicare program for which we have not laid adequate foundations or made complete provision, we are cutting off our nose to spite our face. I say it is absolutely imperative that we give education in all its aspects the first priority so far as our welfare responsibility is concerned.
I would say that our second priority in this area of responsibility concerns health care. But again I say that I do not believe it is the responsibility of the government to assume the health care of all Canadian people. If the Canadian people are what I believe them to be, they want to accept their own responsibilities as they relate to themselves and their families. In the area of government we must accept responsibility through the public purse to take care of those unable to take care of themselves. If we do this we are meeting our over-all responsibility because we will have made available to everyone the health facilities and services we are able to provide. This is our second area of responsibility, so far as priority is concerned, in the general area of welfare.
I would suggest that the third area of welfare in the priority picture is that of pensions, providing for our older people and those who cannot work. What we are doing now is approaching the problem in reverse. We have imposed upon the taxpayer a costly pension plan. It is described as a compulsory saving plan; it is actually a compulsory pension plan. Now we are dealing with medicare. Some time in the near future we will be dealing with education and will get ourselves into trouble. In fact, we are in trouble already in this regard because those concerned with education of whatever kind know very well that the dollar available for education is not 23033-479J
Health and Welfare
adequate. The provincial departments of education, the Teachers' Federation, the ratepayers' associations, are concerned about the fact that they do not have enough money with which to bear the responsibility that is theirs, and the federal government must come in and assist them.
But you cannot solve the problem by pushing it farther from you. There is only the tax dollar available to meet all these charges. Whether it is collected and used by the federal, provincial or local governments does not really matter so far as the taxpayer is concerned, because it is he who pays the tax. Therefore I think it is imperative that in dealing with this legislation we consider the area of priority as it concerns our financial ability to pay through the public purse.
Coming to the points the minister elaborated on today in introducing this resolution, I would make a few comments in the order of his presentation. The minister said the first requirement that will be imposed upon the provincial governments, in relation to their being qualified to receive the 50 per cent contribution from the federal government, is that their medicare schemes provide doctors' services on a universal basis. First of all I believe that the scope is entirely too narrow.
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)
There is a question which I wish to address to the minister and which I think he owes it to us to answer even before the legislation is introduced. Who will set the doctors' fees? The minister says arbitrarily that the plan will cost $28 per capita and the federal government will pay $14 out of that sum, but has the federal government set up a scheme for doctors' fees to which the doctors of Canada and the provincial governments must adhere?

speechtext:
I appreciate the indulgence of hon. members and your own, Mr. Chairman, in permitting me to continue.
My third observation on the first matter raised by the minister concerns our ability to supply adequate numbers of medical practitioners on the basis that is proposed in this legislation. This has already been dealt with in the debate but I think it represents a very real problem.
Experience with medicare programs in Saskatchewan, Great Britain, New Zealand, Sweden and elsewhere has indicated that
immediately the services of medical practitioners are made available on the basis demanded in this legislation the work load of the practitioners is increased. I think that our own inability to increase the number of medical graduates in this country, together with the loss of our graduates through immigration to other countries, in spite of the numbers that arrive here from Great Britain, will pose a very real problem in the implementation of this plan. It is one thing to say we will implement it by July 1, 1967; it is another thing to make it functional on an equitable basis.
Second, we were told this afternoon that any provincial medicare program must give universal coverage but that it will not be compulsory. I find that in this explanation the minister has made a play on words. It seems to me to be practically an exercise in semantics because what could be more compulsory than having to pay for the medicare program through a general tax contribution. In fact it amounts to political blackmail, although I hesitate to use the word because I know the minister, not being that kind of a person, does not really intend it, so far as the provinces are concerned and the individuals as well who do not choose to accept that it is the government's responsibility to meet their own health needs. How can he say it is voluntary if he intends to force the provincial governments to pay for something they are not going to get? It is certainly very compulsory. It includes everyone arbitrarily, whether they need it or not, and therefore to say it is not a compulsory scheme so far as payment is concerned is incorrect.
I have been referring specifically to the financial aspect being made compulsory. It is a good feature of this legislation that the freedom to choose doctors is left up to the provincial authorities and is not made compulsory. I believe it is also a violation of individual rights. I suppose one cannot accept the government's responsibility in areas such as these without sacrificing one's individual rights, but that is really unnecessary. I think other alternatives or approaches might be found to be more satisfactory.
In the third point which the minister made in his statement he referred to the fact that one of the prerequisites of the federal government is that the provincial governments must apply the medical program through provincial plans which are non-profit and subject to public audit. What the minister is actually doing here is wiping out the private

July 12, 1966



carrier. How can a private insurance scheme operate under the qualifications that have been outlined to us this afternoon? An hon. member had just said they are not supposed to do so but why should we accept something that is less efficient and more costly if it can be done another way? I believe that today it is possible, because of the efficiency of private enterprise and with proper government regulation, to supply medicare insurance through private carriers at a more economic rate than can be done through public carriers because, whether we like to admit it or not, the government is the least efficient body in administering such schemes.

subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OF CONTRIBUTIONS TOWARD COST OF INSURED MEDICAL CARE
speechtext: May I ask the hon. member, in connection with his suggestion regarding the relative efficiency of public and private plans, whether he heard the figures on the administrative cost put before the committee earlier today by the hon. member for Bur-naby-Coquitlam?

subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OF CONTRIBUTIONS TOWARD COST OF INSURED MEDICAL CARE
speechtext:
I have certainly heard them but the fact is that when you begin to deal with public administrative costs, much of it is hidden in other services that are not directly related to it. The hon. member for Bumaby-Coquitlam did not say very much about the tremendous escalation of the first projected cost of the Saskatchewan medicare system. Only two years after the system was implemented in Saskatchewan the premium cost had more than doubled. Inherent in this are other charges which are also related to public expense. Perhaps there could be justification for doing it that way if the public purse can afford it. But this is not a proven fact by any means. I do not understand why the minister demands that every provincial government eliminate the private carriers now providing health insurance. Certainly this is not good economy or efficiency so far as the citizens of this nation are concerned.
Time does not permit a lengthy debate on this subject but I should like to say very briefly that portability, as explained by the minister, is very necessary. However, this is something which I think can be worked out without forcing this type of medicare program on the provinces. I believe every provincial health administration realizes it is unfair to implement a provincial medicare scheme that is not transferable. The transferable feature has worked rather well so far as hospital insurance is concerned and I am sure it could be
Health and Welfare
worked so far as medicare is concerned without making it a prerequisite, as in this legislation, although in principle we must accept it. [DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
I believe it would be wrong to criticize the remarks the minister has made this afternoon without offering some alternative proposals. Very briefly, I should like to mention to him another way of achieving the objective which we all agree must be our ultimate goal in the area of health. If the government had said that they were going to be completely responsible for the medical care of pensioners in Canada, they would have relieved provincial health administrations of one of the most costly areas of medical care. Because we are concerned with pensions for our senior citizens, the government could well have said that they were going to extend that pension responsibility to include complete medical coverage for these pensioners.
I believe the provision of medical care is even more essential for these older citizens than increasing the pension to $100 per month. We all know that the most expensive time of our life, in so far as medical costs are concerned, is in our senior years. This would have been an area in which the federal government could have legitimately claimed jurisdiction, and it would have saved provincial departments of health tremendous amounts of money in the implementation of their own medicare programs. I do not believe we have to have uniformity in medicare programs across the country simply because the needs of areas differ.
Another practical way of meeting the increasing costs of medicare would be to supply the provincial governments with a per capita grant. If it were desired to place prerequisites on the making of the grants, it could have been stipulated that they must be used for preventive medicine. They could also have been designated for the care of our children because it is in these areas that preventive medicine offers the greatest opportunity of service.
I would also suggest to the minister that I believe it is the desire of every Canadian citizen to take care of his own needs. Unfortunately there are some who are unable to do so. This is particularly true when some unfortunate accident happens to the family. I am speaking from experience in this connection because throughout the years my father's family had tremendous health costs. 1 remember, as a young school teacher, that my dad took me into the room where he kept his

July 12, 1966
Health and Welfare
records and showed me receipts for more than $10,000 for medical and hospital care. This was at a time when dollars were worth a lot more than now. This burden of medical costs made it difficult for him to provide assistance to those who were fortunate enough to have good health and who wanted an education. There are many families in Canada today who face such a calamity. I believe the one great fear many Canadian parents have in so far as medical costs are concerned is that some unfortunate accident or disease will hit them and they will not have the financial means to meet it.
Thus as a third point I believe the federal government, therefore, could easily justify providing every Canadian family with some form of basic calamity or accident insurance policy which would take care of hospital and medical fees say in excess of $1,000. In summary if the government had proposed such a program that would take care of our senior citizens first, that would assist the provinces in taking care of our school age children or pre-school age children with respect to preventive health care through the provision of a per capita grant or if we had some kind of insurance scheme to take care of extreme cases of accident or disease catastrophe, I think they would have had an alternative so far as their responsibility for medicare is concerned. Then the provinces would be able to take care of the remaining medical costs without placing too great a burden upon them. This is why, Mr. Chairman, I find it very difficult to accept the arguments that have been put forward by the minister today that this is the best method by which our responsibilities in the area of health care can be met.
On the basis of those arguments it is impossible for us to give support to the legislation he is proposing. I do not agree with the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam that this legislation must be dealt with in the next week or two. I hope that if this resolution does pass, as we expect it will even though we cannot give it our support, the legislation will be referred to the proper committee. If it is possible for some of our committees considering major legislative items to meet prior to parliament reconvening, that would be good. I believe therefore that provision must be made before we leave here to send this legislation to a committee for further study. We should not pass the legislation in an autocratic fashion that would deny the provinces

the medical profession and others, the right to make representations before a committee. We should not force something on the provinces which is going to commit them to vast sums of money without the provinces having too much to say about it. I believe, therefore, that as soon as the legislation is introduced it should be referred to the committee for the further study which it deserves and must have.

subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OF CONTRIBUTIONS TOWARD COST OF INSURED MEDICAL CARE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, it is always a pleasure for me to rise to speak in this house, because I am sitting on this side of the house which has always been in the vanguard of Canada's future. We have been given a further proof of this in the last two hours because it seems that hon. members opposite who have taken a position on the measure do not seem to know what medicare is about. Everything was mixed up: socialism, drugs and medicine. It seems to me it might be well advised at times, to consider whether speeches should not be somewhat shorter, but mean something.
We have always been the party of the people. We are the party dealing daily with the needs of the Canadian people and that is why I am doubly pleased to take this opportunity to say a few words about this social security measure which is part of the vast general humane program of my party, I mean medicare as proposed by our government.
The right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) at the federal-provincial conference of July 65, had, as you know, stated that the federal government would financially assist the provinces willing to introduce medicare, provided they meet the four basic requirements or principles which are that the schemes be universal-a much discussed point about which I shall say more later-transferable, that they provide assistance for or, if you prefer, that they include all medical services provided either by practitioners or by specialists, whether in the hospital, in the office or at home and, finally, that such plans be administered by a provincial government or under its responsibility.
Of these four principles, two-transferability of benefits and complete assistance or coverage of all medical services, seem to have been almost unanimously approved by Canadians.
I shall try, as much as possible, to speak today on the two other requirements laid down by my government to help the provinces
July 12, 1966

anxious to attract their citizens, that is universality and public administration. The basic principle underlying the provision of medicare by the government is society's responsibility to provide all citizens with adequate health services.
[DOT] (6:00 p.m.)
Every Canadian citizen has a perfect right to complete and continued protection. That is a basic human right like the right to education, life and freedom. The government cannot divest itself of its responsibilities by relying on the administration of private enterprises, whatever they may be, for profitable purposes or not. Physical health, like mental health, is equally important in remaining able to work, in holding a remunerative job. Furthermore, it is essential to the economic security of a nation; if an army's victory depends on a full stomach, the economic prosperity of a country depends on the health of its citizens.
Anyway, why should private companies be interested in the administration of a program on a non-profit basis, which would be the only acceptable way? These companies would have to see some advantage in it, for example publicity for their life insurance company, because many such companies were established for non-profitable purposes simply to have free publicity throughout the country. I do not see how these public funds can be used to this end, even in such an indirect way.
The federal government undertakes to pay 50 per cent of the cost of this program and must see to it that this money is used to provide protection for all its citizens on equal terms and conditions throughout Canada. Under the circumstances, in my humble opinion, only a public administration system can give the government this assurance without burdening the administrative machinery to no purpose with a control which is increasingly difficult to maintain and a nuisance to all.
Universal application, as the hon. Minister of Health and Welfare (Mr. MacEachen) said several times, means that at least 90 per cent of the population of a province must be covered for the moment by the provincial program, again under uniform conditions and without differentiation as to age, financial position or ill health.
In a few years this 90 per cent of the population will become close to 100 per cent, the figure we are to reach. In my opinion, the government is wise to insist on this universal application, for, as I said earlier, it
Health and Welfare
is responsible for the health of every individual, for humanitarian and economic reasons. The financial barrier which prevents many people from receiving medical care, affects not only the individual himself but all of society.
A person's illness creates a social void around him which affects not only his near relations but all society. It creates general disorder.
The question of the famous arguments, that is, whether the provinces are ready to receive the compulsory health insurance program called medicare, may be raised. Some sharp discussions have already taken place, but the government was wise enough, before entering this field, to appoint a commission called the Hall commission to inquire into health services in Canada and their needs.
Now, this commission which looked into the matter for almost three years, studied health needs and sought means to extend and improve present services, reached the same conclusion. It recommended a universal plan on a public management basis. All members of the commission seconded this recommendation, including doctors, nurses, dentists and even a former president of the Canadian Medical Association, an organization which comprises approximately 75 per cent of all Canadian doctors.
I feel that in the present situation, especially as I pointed out earlier, it rests with the government to provide for education and health services. It is up to the government to provide the required funds so that no Canadian in 1967 is deprived of the bare minimum, including health.
And I know that in this very house, on August 22, 1958, when hospital insurance began to take shape in the province of Quebec, it was said that that province would only participate in a hospital insurance plan, as stated by the member for Quebec West:
When we have beds for the sick.
It was only two years later that the province of Quebec, with the same number of beds or almost, went down to history as being the last to participate in the Canadian hospital plan, after losing approximately $154 million in benefits.
I shall now give a brief historical account of what has taken place in Canada over a good many years.

The interest which all provinces now have in public health insurance began first in the

July 12. 1966
Health and Welfare
western provinces of Canada and in Newfoundland. While the legislature of British Columbia was probably the first to consider the issue of health insurance with the appointment of a royal commission in 1919, the first action was taken in the prairie provinces during and after world war I with the operation of the union hospital and municipal doctor systems, and in Newfoundland with the introduction of the cottage hospital system in 1934.
Further action was taken by several provinces during the period 1943 to 1949. In Quebec in 1943 an act to constitute a health insurance commission was passed. The commission was directed to study the problem of health insurance and to suggest a plan. However, in 1945 the legislation was repealed and the work was terminated. The Municipal Health Services Act was passed in Ontario in 1944 to enable municipalities to develop contributory plans subject to approval of the provincial department of health for whatever medical care services were required.
Under the Health Services Act of 1945 Manitoba made provision for the extension of health services and for the organization of medical care districts in which, subject to approval of the Minister of Health, municipalities could enter into contracts with physicians for specified, prepaid medical care. A Health Services Act was passed in Saskatchewan in 1945 to provide comprehensive health services including hospital, medical and dental services, and pharmaceutical benefits for persons receiving old age pensions, mothers' allowances, and general welfare. Beginning in 1946, under the same legislation the Swift Current health region operated a universal, prepaid, public medical care service for residents of that area.
The Saskatchewan hospital services plan began operation in 1947. It was the first provincial program to provide comprehensive, prepaid hospital insurance on a compulsory basis to almost the entire population. Alberta introduced a maternity hospital care program in 1944 and the Alberta hospital services plan in 1949, which were available without charge to all residents. The British Columbia hospital insurance service began also in 1949 in that province.
Public medical care insurance plans are presently in operation in seven provinces: Newfoundland, Manitoba, Ontario, Quebec, Saskatchewan, Alberta, and British Columbia. Newfoundland provides coverage for medical and surgical care to part of the population,

under the cottage hospital medical care plan. In Manitoba, under the provisions of the Health Services Act, 1945, voluntary, prepaid coverage is available in organized medical care districts for medical care specified in contracts between physicians and municipalities. Since 1962 Saskatchewan has been operating a province-wide, compulsory medical care insurance program. The Swift Current regional medical care insurance plan conti-ues in contract with the medical care insurance commission of the province. Public programs for the provision of voluntary medical insurance to any resident have been in operation in Alberta since 1963, and in British Columbia since 1965. Ontario has amended its legislation passed in 1965 and has scheduled a plan of voluntary coverage for any resident which commenced operation on July 1, 1966. Quebec accepted a modified health plan for its social beneficiaries last April. It is presently studying a medical care insurance plan and the provincial government has expressed its intention to introduce a plan by January 1, 1968.
[DOT] (6:10 p.m.)
The three maritime provinces of New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island have not taken any independent action to plan or introduce public medical care insurance except that at the conference of federal and provincial ministers of health, held in Ottawa on February 1, 1966, New Brunswick accepted the federal proposals but Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island did not make any commitment on these proposals for health insurance. Maybe Prince Edward Island will change its mind after what happened yesterday.
The first recorded official interest of the federal government in health insurance was in 1928 when the standing committee on industrial and international relations was authorized to investigate and report on insurance against unemployment, sickness and disability. Their recommendations culminated in the Employment and Social Insurance Act, 1935, which provided for the appointment of a commission to gather information on health insurance plans and to submit to the Governor in Council proposals for federal cooperation in the provision of benefits. The act was subsequently declared unconstitutional by the Supreme Court and the Privy Council.
More thorough study of the issue began in 1941 when the minister of pensions and national health presented a report on the deficiencies in public health and medical services
July 12, 1966

in Canada to the annual meeting of the Dominion Council of Health. The members were sympathetic to the formulation of a plan for health insurance. A study was then launched, with that objective, under the direction of the department of pensions and national health. The Canadiana Medical Association formed a committee on health insurance to assist in the preparation of a draft plan for public health and health insurance. The outcome of this study was a draft bill which was reported to the House of Commons on July 29, 1944. It was discussed with provincial ministers and deputy ministers of health in May of that year. The federal proposal based on the bill was presented to the dominion-provincial conference on reconstruction convened in 1945. The proposal included a comprehensive health insurance program supported in part by federal contribution and administered by the provinces, health grants to improve public health services throughout Canada, and loans to assist and promote the construction of hospitals. However, discussion at the conference centred mainly on financial arrangements and taxation. Since all provinces failed to reach agreement with the federal government on those arrangements, adoption of the proposed national health program was precluded.
In the following years parts of the federal proposal of 1945 were separately put into effect. The national health grant program was introduced in 1948 to provide grants in aid of public health services, health surveys, professional training, and hospital construction. Then the Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act was passed in 1957. By the end of 1960 agreements had been made with all provinces and territories to make the program national in scope.
On June 20, 1961, the Royal Commission on Health Services was appointed with Chief Justice Emmett M. Hall as chairman. By Order in Council P.C. 1961-883 the commission was required to inquire into and report upon the existing facilities and the future need for health services for the people of Canada and the resources to provide such services, and to recommend such measures, consistent with the constitutional division of legislative powers in Canada, as the commissioners believe will ensure that the best possible health care is available to all Canadians. The commission's report was tabled in the House of Commons on June 19,
Health and Welfare
1964. This report further focused the attention of the federal government on the desirability of some system of nation-wide medical care insurance.
Subsequently, at the federal-provincial conference held in Ottawa in July, 1965, the federal government made certain proposals to bring about a system of health insurance in all provinces by a target date of July 1, 1967. During the meeting of provincial and federal ministers of health in Ottawa on February 1, 1966, three provinces accepted the federal proposals and the others remained uncommitted without making any definite refusal of the offer. In reviewing the situation the federal Minister of National Health and Welfare hoped that all provinces would accept the proposals by the target date.

This shows, Mr. Chairman, that since 1919, for nearly 50 years, Canada has been seeking some solution for the conservation of the health of the individual. The Hall Commission has concretized this desire for medical care offered to every Canadian.
Many will say that conflicts will arise between physicians and patients. I do not think so. I think that even if we do not have yet the necessary material for the task which is shortly to be ours, and if we must make a superhuman effort, perhaps when these programs are implemented, I am speaking of physicians eventually, everything will level off. With our professional and technical training and health resources program, toward which the federal government put aside $500 million to develop that manpower of technicians, nurses, medical research centres, new universities which will train more physicians, everything will be phased-in, as was the case for hospital insurance. I am speaking of the province of Quebec and of a need its people wants to be fulfilled.

We must do it for the sake of our fellow-citizens, for the sake of our present government which is always ready, as it has always been in the past, to practise its theory of liberalism which consists in serving those in need, those who need its assistance.
This comes within the general implementation of social welfare programs and leads the way toward their fullest application in the near future.
Medicare will be the greatest piece of legislation ever undertaken by any government, since it will affect personally and directly each and everyone of 20 million Canadian citizens.
I ask the medical profession, to which I have the honour to belong, to be courageous as it has always been since the beginning of medical history, in order to prove to the other citizens that we are worthy of our forefathers, who worked without cease under .extremely difficult conditions to accomplish the most humanitarian task, that of caring for one's fellow-men, so that they might enjoy the greatest gift all-health.
Before closing, Mr. Chairman, let me tell those who say that Canada is not ready for a medicare program that the same thing happened in 1958. At that time, the Canadian hospitals, having only a limited number of beds, were not ready to accept the hospital insurance plan. I have before me a book which dates back to 1895, where the doctors of that time are advised to study so as to keep up with the progress of science in the last 15 years, that is since 1880. The doctors are asked to go back to university so as to be up to date. If the doctors of that time had followed this advice, they would have been forced to close their offices and their patients would have died while they were studying. We should not postpone indefinitely the establishment of the medicare plan in Canada, because it must come into operation in 1967. People are asking for it.

Mr. Chairman, with reference to the remarks made by the preceding speaker I congratulate him on the simple and abiding faith he seems to have. I only wish I had it. It may be that he sits in a different position than I do, and maybe he has not been here as long, but I hope he can continue to have that sort of faith. It is very touching.
I intend to make reference later to some of the comments of the hon. member for Simcoe East, who made a tremendous contribution to this debate. So far as the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam is concerned, he said what was predictable, and I think what he said was mostly wrong. There is one thing about the hon. member. When he is wrong he is consistently wrong whereas, in contrast, the government is usually wrong but it is usually inconsistently wrong.
The hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam spoke of the necessity of staying here to complete all stages of this legislation. The minister did not go quite that far. He was not quite that ambitious. He is prepared to make three or four bites of the cherry, and indicated a lurking desire to finish second reading.
There is, Mr. Chairman, no monopoly of political virtue in any part of this chamber. I am prepared, as I am convinced is each other member of this party, to stay in session if it is necessary. However, not only is it not necessary but it is quite undesirable that we should deal with any more than resolution stage at this time.
Despite the considerable finesse exercised by the minister when glossing over what 1 think are some compulsive features which will be embodied in this legislation, there are these aspects of it. The hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam said that there has been a royal commission preceding this legislation and there had been studies and surveys made which generated a lot of comment. So far as royal commissions are concerned, we have so many of them that when Canadians hear about a report of another royal commission they usually hide their heads under a pillow. But that is not the point. This debate should be on a national scale.
July 12, 1966

There are interests involved of provincial governments, of professional institutions, of hospitals and municipalities, and over and above that there are the interests of every person in Canada. It is my sincere view that when the resolution is passed and the bill is exposed it is desirable we should stop there so that the contents of the bill may become fully known. The minister knows what is in the bill. So far as he could he gave us some indication of what it contains, but it is a condition precedent to any further debate that during the course of the summer there should be an opportunity for the people of Canada to inquire into this measure, to formulate their views about it and pass those views on to their members of parliament who in turn can debate the measure. In that way we could make a greater, more interesting and more valid contribution when we return in the fall, and so I cannot go along with the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam on that suggestion.
As a matter of fact, Mr. Chairman, my views are very much the same as those of the hon. member for Red Deer, with whom I do not always agree. It may be that the Chinook winds which originate in Calgary and blow up to Red Deer sometimes get as far as Peace River, but many of the things he has said are comments with which I find myself in agreement, especially those concerning welfare.
The phrase contained in the American Declaration of Independence, "life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness," has been translated in this country by this government as "life and the pursuit of welfare." Welfare, in its broadest sense and ordinary meaning, is fine, but the narrower, restrictive and artificial interpretation which is now all too often accepted is something else entirely.
Any step which is directed against the triple evils of poverty, disease and ignorance must of necessity be of overriding concern to any legislative body, but this does not relieve us of the obligation to scrutinize measures like this with the greatest of care. Not only must we look at the merits of the proposal itself but at its relationship to the national interest and the over-all economy.
As to the intrinsic merits certainly the Hall report, at first blush, appears to be ample authority. Any reader of this report will find a carefully documented argument, well buttressed with supporting material. To take the report by itself, one would be hard put to find reasons to oppose it but, set in the context of the contemporary political, social,
Health and. Welfare
and economic background, I have some misgivings which I must voice.
The minister has given us some hint, although it is not in terms of the report, of the cost of the scheme in terms of the federal contribution. To this we must add the provincial costs. One wonders about the validity of these figures. The original estimates prepared for almost all government proposals, for the great public works starting with the building of the railroads down to the building of the St. Lawrence Seaway, have always been greatly exceeded. In addition, there are the maintenance and annual carrying charges which are always substantially greater than estimated. This applies also to most of the social welfare schemes which we have introduced in Canada, and these costs are reflected in increased taxes-income, excise, sales, customs and property-a cost which is borne by the small consumer in two forms.
In the first place, it is an inescapable fact that as a result of the proven extravagance, waste and bad management in government the taxpayer's dollar when returned to him in the form of benefits has decreased when passing through the government establishment. Conversely, the cost is further increased because that portion of the public which has the opportunity to pass on the increased taxes paid always manages to do so in such a way, and with such an increment, that the aggregate of the amount passed on, in higher costs of goods and services, invariably exceeds what has been contributed in the form of taxes, and so there is a loss at both ends.
[DOT] (6:30 p.m.)
In the orthodox inflationary consideration, higher taxes mean higher prices, higher prices require higher wage levels, and sometimes there are strikes and work stoppages to obtain these with all the loss of production and confusion that follows. This in turn involves still higher prices with demands for more government-sponsored assistance, increases in pensions and so on. There is an ever-increasing, dizzy, upward spiral. Ask any housewife who goes to the supermarket to do her shopping. The improved standard of living and the related collateral social benefits that we all desire then become a mirage held out for us on the one hand- pension plan, assistance programs, medicare, higher wages-but then snatched away on the other by the fantastic increases we have to pay for everything needed for the ordinary business of living.

July 12, 1965
Health and Welfare
Social programs must be or ought to be financed out of increased national productivity. Surely there should be some relation between the quantum of such benefits and the index of our productivity. Unfortunately Canada has a top-heavy three level government structure, national, provincial and municipal, and with a tax system frequently operating to stultify incentive has been dispensing social welfare and wage increases without too much regard to its ability as a nation to pay for them out of increased productivity.
As a nation we seem to have acquired an infinite capacity for self-deception on this score. Certainly the capacity has been fostered and nurtured by the present government which gives the people a series of temporary palliatives, something to keep them momentarily content without regard to the ultimate cost. I think it is about time for some real sincerity and honesty, a time for a government to say: Here is the benefit if you desire it but here is the cost. Certainly this is what the Hall Commission suggested. I do not know what the minister will do in this regard, but recommendation No. 194 at page 88 of the Hall Royal Commission report reads as follows:
That taxes collected by the federal government to pay for the expanded health services program be identified in such a manner as to make it clear to the taxpayer that the taxes paid cover the health service benefits made available to him.
I hope this will be in the bill when it is introduced.
The case which the government makes is as usual nothing but its stock of shop-worn cliches cunningly interwoven with the selfadulation which is the trade mark of the Liberal party. Rather than concentrating on baking a bigger and better pie, it has become obsessed with the task of trying to divide and subdivide the existing one.
I have tried to give some idea of the price we pay. What do we get in return? There is a guarantee of adequate medical care for those who might not otherwise have this benefit. We must, of course, consider this in terms of the shortage of personnel needed to provide this care. Here I should like to make a very brief comment in respect of the remarks of the hon. member for Simcoe East. Here is a man who obviously is sincere and who has made a powerful contribution to this debate. He is a man who is on the firing line in this fight to provide health services, and he tells us honestly and sincerely of his fears for the

future in the light of what he feels the government may have in mind. I do not think it is possible for anyone who heard the hon. member for Simcoe East to dismiss lightly the cautions and warnings he has uttered.
It is a very desirable and laudable objective to drive away the spectre of fear and the burden of having to endure the indignities and the misery and pain of illness which is susceptible to treatment and help. Certainly we must move to achieve this objective. The question is whether the government in its bill will provide a proposal which is acceptable without change and whether it can advance persuasive arguments that are logical that the scheme it proposes must be taken in its total form. It is my view, Mr. Chairman, that the time has come to take a stand, not necessarily a stand against the establishment of a program to provide a better medical health program in Canada but a stand that such programs, and all other social welfare programs, be dealt with with due regard to the essential priorities, with due regard to the impact they have on the life of people, and with due regard to the inflationary aspect of our economy. I have apprehensions about the slap-happy, haphazard, helter-skelter programs which this government has been introducing with more emphasis on political advantages than on proper planning.
I think we must consider our ability to finance these things. I am not speaking in terms of cost in dollars but rather in terms of the deteriorating dollar and in terms of the continuing diminishing amount which the doRar buys today. That is the consideration which I fear and which I have in mind. We must also think in terms of the necessity to provide adequate national savings in the form of real wealth for these programs as weR as other essential programs which I see in relation to our need for increased productivity such as the development of national resources, improvements to our national transportation system, education generally, as well as increases in the productive skills of labour forces, increases in technological improvements required in respect of industry and so on. In addition we must be prepared to increase sharply our external aid to developing nations, not only to help them but in enlightened self-interest.
So, without opposing this resolution at this time until I have an opportunity to see, digest and discuss the legislation, I think it is essential that there be an objective and impartial survey and evaluation of our position
July 12, 1966

vis-a-vis the use of our resources, one that should be made outside of government on a non-political basis.
I therefore have considered and suggest an amendment as follows:
"The said act shall not come into operation until such time as the Economic Council of Canada has made a report to parliament and to the government as to the relative priority in terms of time and capital to be assigned to present and proposed social welfare programs and such other measures as are required to develop productive capacity to provide for these and other requirements of the people, the said report to be made by July 1, 1967".
I am quite prepared to say, Mr. Chairman, that there may be some question about the amendment being in order. I am not going to make an argument on that now, but I propose it in order to emphasize the point of view I have been making. I feel that the Economic Council, a body independent of government which already through its reports has made a study of the over-all pattern of government costs and expenditures with relation to the price structure and productive capacity, is the proper body. Such a survey should examine these various proposals from the economic point of view including a study of the contribution they make and the extent to which they affect the price structure so that the net value and net worth of these programs can be assessed.
It is not my intention to suggest that the Economic Council should assume the responsibility of the government. Parliament and the government can never abdicate their sole responsibility in this regard. It is always for the government to initiate and for parliament to legislate these programs. But it is now apparent that we should provide ourselves with the best available information and that this requires at the present time a survey of the economy to see what effect these measures will have and to see what can be done to contain the price structure. I say quite sincerely that this is not necessarily a position in opposition to the measure. It will require a study of the terms set out in the bill to form an opinion in that regard.
In my view, however, we have failed to recognize the cumulative and pyramiding result that all such programs have on the general economic situation and the eroding effect on the financial position of the majority of Canadians, for example, those who have fixed incomes and farmers whose income is established by external conditions. This is on the assumption which we are entitled to make that no action or inadequate action is
Health and Welfare
being taken to develop our productive capacity to stabilize price levels.
[DOT] (6:40 p.m.)
There is an Alice In Wonderland quality, or at least a great deal of hypocrisy, in the position of the federal government. We pass these various measures I have mentioned and thereby set a bad example in our extravagance in government. We provide, even initiate, wage increases without regard to sound basic guidelines. We shirk our duty to increase productivity. As a result of these factors or at least in large part because of them, when prices go up we complain in this house and elsewhere and we mumble about price control.
Even if imposed price controls ever make political and economic sense we have absolutely no jurisdiction to tamper directly with these controls. We are limited to the indirect method of fiscal and monetary steps. We set in motion inflationary forces; we inject their pressure into our economic system and then we whine and whimper about the results. For this reason it seems to me that such unbiased, non-political report should be available before we proceed. There would be no interference with the procedure of legislation.
If it should happen, Mr. Chairman, that the minister is impressed by the comments I have made, perhaps we could design the amendment I have moved in such a way as to satisfy him.
