Order. With regard to the relevancy of the amendment now before the committee, it seems to the Chair that the amendment goes beyond the provisions of the resolution. Therefore it would appear irrelevant to the resolution and as such the amendment would be out of order. May I also suggest that the amendment fails on other grounds in that it is declaratory of principle and is in the nature of a reasoned amendment. The authority for this ruling is to be found at page 798 of May's seventeenth edition, chapter XXIX, headed "Expenditure: Financial Resolutions. Procedure in Committee of the Whole House on Expenditure." The paragraph headed "Scope of Debate on Resolution" reads as follows:
Debate in committee on a financial resolution is confined to the terms of the resolution itself and must not be extended to the related bill.
The next section, headed "Procedure on Amendments", says:
The approval or the reduction of the expenditure under consideration, or an increase in the stringency of the terms and conditions of the charge thereby created, are the matters specially entrusted to such a committee, and to these objects amendments are directed.
An amendment proposing to substitute for the resolution an argumentative justification for the refusal of the demand is out of order-
On these grounds I regret that I must declare this amendment out of order.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OF CONTRIBUTIONS TOWARD COST OF INSURED MEDICAL CARE
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, first I should like to congratulate the minister and the government for bringing forward this very important measure at this time. I should particularly like to congratulate the minister because I think that in the relatively short time he has held this office he has done a remarkable job.

subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OF CONTRIBUTIONS TOWARD COST OF INSURED MEDICAL CARE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OF CONTRIBUTIONS TOWARD COST OF INSURED MEDICAL CARE
speechtext:
A great many people in this country have been talking about medicare for a long time and have often been very glib about the subject. It is one which involves several jurisdictions, not the least of which is the provincial jurisdiction, and action in this connection tends to tread on many toes. The minister has effectively carried out his negotiations with the provinces. As a result of his efforts the provincial governments know where the federal government stands in this respect, and I am quite sure that the medical
Health and Welfare
profession and many other people associated with the provision of health care in this country now have a much better idea of where we are heading than has ever been the case in the past. I am quite sure they have a much better idea, for example, than had the professional people in the province of Saskatchewan a few years ago when the previous Saskatchewan government's medicare plan was brought in there.
I want to concentrate briefly on some of the financial aspects of this plan, but first I would say that medicare, in the sense of this resolution and later the bill, rounds out the number of vital health care services which we badly need in this country. We had the health grants legislation back in the late 1940's. We had hospital insurance brought in by federal legislation in 1957. It has been eminently successful. One fact attesting to this is that close to 100 per cent, of the order of 99 per cent, of all Canadians are now covered in respect of hospital insurance.
We have had passed more recently under the present minister the health resources plan which will help to provide many of the professional people and, more importantly in connection with the present legislation, the doctors who will be required to supply the needs of the country in respect of physicians' services.
Now we have the medicare legislation to provide for the paying of doctors' bills throughout the country. There is an old saying that goes something along these lines: A man or a woman is really well off when he or she is healthy, wealthy and wise. Personally I would rate good health ahead of being wealthy. I suggest that good health also precedes being wise, because I cannot imagine a child who is suffering from some disease learning very well and I cannot imagine an individual of more advanced years who is suffering from some ailment being very rational or wise. So I think that in the order of priorities we are dealing with something that is vital, something which heads the list. I would disagree at least to this extent with the hon. member for Red Deer who suggested that education should come ahead of health, because I believe that the reverse order is probably true. Certainly as a matter of emphasis I would put health well up the list. I would even put it ahead of wealth and wisdom in the priority of things.
The minister has passed over this matter rather lightly but I have heard other speakers say quite often that health is a matter of

July 12, 1966
Health and Welfare
provincial responsibility. I do not want to agree with that conclusion. Indeed, I have yet to be convinced that health is a subject which is totally a matter of provincial responsibility. I tend to believe the contrary. I believe that because health is so important it is something which is to the general advantage of Canada. I have not found a specific clause in the British North America Act, our constitution, which says that the nation must have little or nothing to do with health, and I notice that we have a federal Department of National Health and Welfare which has survived under two different administrations. Therefore I suggest that health is to a degree at least an important federal or national responsibility.
This legislation is essentially financial in character. It deals with money. It does not deal, at least in any great detail, with the administration of a medicare plan. The administration in its depth and detail will be a matter for the provinces. This measure says in effect that the government of Canada, the representatives of the people of Canada here in parliament assembled, will collect from all the people of Canada a given sum of money every year and will distribute it equally to all Canadians. The government here in Ottawa will remit to each provincial government a given sum of money which reflects the population in that province.
The formula is arrived at roughly in this way. The sum total of all doctors' bills is properly checked out, properly accounted. They are totalled, divided by the Canadian population and a certain figure is arrived at. The estimate for next year is of the order of $34 per capita. The total doctors' bill for Canada is $34 multiplied by 20 million, being the number of people in Canada. That is $680 million as the total bill for next year.
The federal government, as I understand it, under the proposed legislation will pay half that amount, half of $34 or $17 per person, to the provincial governments. Each province will receive its population figure times $17 for that year. The province from which I come, with a population approaching two million, would therefore receive two million times $17 or close to $34 million, or about 5 per cent of the total national cost of medicare or 10 per cent of the total federal tax collection for and expenditures on medicare. Some provinces might find their costs a little higher than $34 on the average, some less, but they will receive $17 per capita and will have a genuine incentive to average out at around the Canadian average figure.

[DOT] (7:00 pm.)
They will indeed have an incentive to cut the cost. In some of the provinces, such as Ontario and British Columbia, where hourly
wage rates, and other prices are higher, the figure may be above $34-maybe $36 or $40-but $17 per capita will come back to that province from the national treasury. This is a measure which, to some degree, spreads the wealth across the nation. It is a measure which collects from all of those who pay the federal income tax, the federal corporation tax, the federal sales tax, import duties and so on. It collects from those who can afford to pay and it redistributes the moneys on a per capita basis across the country. I therefore say it is a measure which, in some degree redistributes wealth across the nation.
That is as it should be, and I am quite convinced that the people of British Columbia, the people in my riding, who perhaps on the average are better off than the average Canadian, would go along with this legislation. They also recognize health care as being one of the top priority items in this country, if not the highest priority item. They are quite willing to pay according to their ability and to see these moneys distributed more in accordance with the needs of individual Canadians across the country, with the needs of those who are less fortunate, those who are ill, who suffer from accidents, and so on.
I would now like to say a word about rising costs, because a great deal of nonsense has been said about the extent of the increase of costs of medicare. We hear references to the fact that the bill for medicare in the United Kingdom has gone up five or six times since the end of world war II, since medicare was brought in by the Labour government in the late 1940's. This is true in dollar terms, but the cost of medical care, of physicians' services in this country has also gone up five or six times.
As I recall it, the national income of Canada at the end of world war II was around $12 billion; today it is over $50 billion. Our national income has gone up fivefold and the percentage of that income devoted to physicians' services has risen, not fallen. I therefore suggest that the total of all the bills collected by the physicians in this country has risen five or six times.
This is not wrong; this is as it should be. However, let us face the fact that in a country such as the United Kingdom an increase of
July 12. 1966

five or six times has its parallel in Canada which, so far at least, has not had a comprehensive prepaid medical care plan.
The Hall Commission found that, on the average, countries which were industrialized and enjoyed a reasonably high standard of living spent anywhere between 4.5 and 5.5 per cent of their national income on health services of different kinds. In 1961 the United Kingdom spent around 5 per cent, while we spent 5.4 per cent. It follows that without a comprehensive, prepaid medical care scheme we were devoting more of our national income to health care than were the people of the United Kingdom. Today our percentage is comparable to or higher than that of other nations such as west Germany, and the Scandinavian countries which have had such universal schemes in effect, not just for years but for decades. I would even venture to say that in the case of Germany this type of scheme has been in effect for nearly a century. We find that those countries were able to develop a medical profession which is among the best in the world and which performs services that are satisfactory to the people of those countries.
It is typical that as the income of the people rises, they spend more on medical services. So we should not be surprised to see the percentage devoted to medical care of physicians' services in this country rise over the next few years. However, there is a point beyond which, as people become more affluent, the percentage goes over a threshold so to speak. It begins to fall after people pass the $5,000 a year income level. By the time they get up to around $10,000 the share falls to 3 or 4 per cent. If all Canadians were suddenly propelled into the $10,000 a year income bracket, we would not be spending 5.5 to 6 per cent on health services, as we are currently doing, but a lesser amount. The prospect therefore is for an increase in percentage for some time, then a levelling off, then a decline in the payments.
I have noticed that the minister made some allowance for a sharp increase in the demand for physicians' services in the first year or two. This is in accordance with experience in other countries. Many people, 10 or 15 per cent of the population, are afraid of going to a doctor because of the bills they will encounter, or else they put off going to a doctor for so long that they never get to one at all. Under a medical care plan these people will be more inclined to go to a physician and have the benefit of his advice and his care.
Health and Welfare
There will therefore be an increase in the workload of the medical profession in this country. There is no point in trying to ignore this fact. The demand is there, the human factor is there, and surely as members of parliament will recognize, the need is there. If the medical profession is not adequately staffed today, and in some cases does not have adequate research facilities, hospital equipment and so on, then it is our responsibility to make sure that opportunities are given for training, the carrying on of research, and that the necessary facilities are provided for them. There will be a period of some difficulty; an increase in the workload is bound to cause some strain. But this is a type of strain which the great majority of the medical profession is not only prepared to accept, but is willing and anxious to meet to the best of its ability.
Not long ago I came across the brief of the Canadian Medical Association to the Hall Commission. It stated the following as the objectives of the doctors of Canada:
1.	The highest standard of medical services should be available to every resident of Canada.
2.	Insurance to prepay the costs of medical services should be available to all regardless of age, state of health or financial status.
3.	Certain individuals require assistance to pay medical services insurance costs.
4.	The efforts of organized medicine, governments, and all other interested bodies should be co-ordinated toward these ends.
These recommendations, which seem to fit amazingly well into the resolution we have before us-and I trust the legislation will be forthcoming-arise out of the predicament in which many individuals find themselves. You and I may well have experienced a situation such as this.
I wish to quote from a book which appeared some time ago written by Henry Richardson entitled "Economic and Financial Aspects of Social Security". It states:
Sickness is too uncertain and irregular in its onset and too variable in its severity for the cost to be met as it occurs out of the normal family budget. Provision can be made effectively only by saving, but many people do not make adequate savings individually, especially if their means are low, and young people may not have had time to save enough to pay for a severe and costly illness. Moreover, medical care is becoming increasingly costly because of the advances being made in scientific research and techniques. In consequence, the difficulty of paying direct for medical care has become much greater and will continue to increase. The remedy is for the risks of sickness to be pooled by the whole community and for medical needs to be met mainly by small regular payments from the family's annual budget.

July 12, 1966
Health and Welfare
I should now like to refer to some of the benefits. The Hall Commission considered this matter, but I am sure the Economic Council also, if the hon. member for Peace River had been successful, would not only have investigated expenditures but would also have looked into the benefits which would result from better and improved medical care. They would have dealt with facts of this nature. On the average, roughly 2 per cent of our working force is absent through illness all the time. These people who are off for extended periods of time, if they had continued to be productive and had better care, could have, increased our national income by about 4 per cent. Even if we had an increase of half of one per cent, if we could knock the incidence of illness down by about 10 per cent-a half of one per cent relative to 4 per cent-then we could more than offset any possible increase in the cost of medicare in this country. So the Economic Council, working out the benefits and costs, I am quite sure would come down on the side of an effective prepaid medical care scheme in this country. In other words, I feel a careful economic appraisal would result in a verdict in favour of the introduction of medical care.
[DOT] (7:10 p.m.)
I have referred to the fact that on a number of occasions the minister has underlined the fact that administration is by the provinces, that the details are up to the provinces. The provinces will receive their per capita payments annually. They will collect their own taxes and perhaps will collect premiums as well. The sum total of these revenues will pay the doctors' bills and the provinces will be responsible for the payment of those bills.
There are four important conditions which have been repeatedly stressed by the Prime Minister at federal-provincial conferences and by the minister on a number of occasions. These are conditions attached by the federal government before federal money will be available to the provinces. They are simple, but they are very important. The first concerns the scope of services available. All doctor's services should be available to all Canadians who rely on this type of support, that is all physicians' services must be available to those individuals participating in this plan. This is No. 1.
The second point is that there will be universal coverage, that is, universal in the sense of 90 per cent, originally, and 95 per cent after a period of years. I think that if

our experience in medicare parallels our experience in hospital insurance, this figure will move up toward 98 per cent or 99 per cent. The reasons will become more obvious as we gain experience with this program.
The third point is that the programs must be publicly administered by the provinces. Those provinces may have a variety of schemes. I think this is co-operative federalism working at its best. The federal government agrees to attach a minimum of strings to moneys of this kind, but the strings or conditions are vital to a successful scheme. They involve a minimum of federal direction and they involve a minimum of inconvenience to the provinces, as well as a maximum of flexibility to improve the efficiency of the scheme.
The provinces must take full responsibility themselves. As I understand it, what is meant by public administration is that there must be a minister of health in the province. He and his department must take full responsibility for the soundness of the schemes, whether there be one province-wide, government administered scheme such as presently exists in Saskatchewan, or a multiplicity of schemes which involves one substantial government plan and a variety of other plans. As I understand it, the condition attached is that these additional plans, which may be loosely referred to as private plans, must be in the nature of non-profit operations. They will be thoroughly scrutinized and, in a sense, licensed by the provincial authorities.
Obviously, the doctors' non-profit plans will qualify. I have not discussed this with the minister, but I believe some of the big insurance companies schemes would also qualify, if they are not making a profit? As I understand it, insurance companies have often used medical care insurance as a loss leader to attract attention of the community to their other services. If in fact, they are offering this type of service, I cannot see why they would not qualify as a non-profit operation.

subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OF CONTRIBUTIONS TOWARD COST OF INSURED MEDICAL CARE
speechtext:
I was talking about the private carriers operating as non-profit organizations, in the economic and financial sense of the word. I think it is desirable, and in some provinces I would like to see what these other agencies can do. I should like to see what private insurance companies can do from the standpoint of a non-profit scheme. I noted that recently the London Life Insurance Company, for instance, took the contract for Physicians' Services for the civil service of Ontario away from P.S.I. They took it away from P.S.I. because they had lower costs; they were better organized and they used the latest data processing techniques. Because of their lower costs they made a more attractive bid to the government of Ontario.
I can envisage in this country the possibility of certain provinces having provincially run schemes, and other provinces with a variety of public and private agencies. This flexibility is desirable. If the private agencies are inefficient, they are going to lose out in competition; they are not going to quote the best prices and they are going to be ignored. In any case, I am prepared to take that chance. I think this is a flexible approach, and I believe it is a highly desirable one.
I should have liked to go on at length about the freedom of the individual to choose his doctor, to work wherever he wants in this country and still benefit under the plan. I should have liked even more to talk about the freedom of the doctor to accept any patient or to deny services to that patient. This is the program, as it is evolving, at least in so far as our federal stipulations are concerned. It does not interfere with the doctor in the way the program in the United Kingdom and some other countries does. It does not require a doctor to go to a certain area, to have a panel to serve. It does not limit his freedom in that important sense. He is in no way a civil servant. He is a professional, completely on his own, as he has always been. He may have fewer problems collecting his bills, but I cannot think of any great difficulties he is likely to encounter. Indeed in the remarks made by a number of my doctor friends, some of whom are very vocal and some even hostile, I find a situation similar to that which I encounter when I talk to some of our separatists: They have a problem, but they will not tell us what the solution is. They will not tell us how the constitution can be changed, but they have a problem. Many of those inside and outside the medical profession who are concerned
Health and Welfare
with these imaginary problems will also find that they will disappear when this legislation is implemented.

subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OF CONTRIBUTIONS TOWARD COST OF INSURED MEDICAL CARE
speechtext:
I have listened with a great deal of interest to many of those who have taken part in this debate. I have listened to the hon. member for Coast-Capilano assure the medical profession that they have nothing to fear, that they know exactly where they are going. I suggest to the hon. member that he get together with the Minister of National Health and Welfare to straighten out exactly what their views are, because I distinctly heard the minister say, in relation to the scope of the benefits, that the government was going to see that all the services provided by the physicians were insured services. He went further to say that they were going to insure the availability of physicians' services.
If hon. members do not believe that is a problem, then they do not know what went on in Saskatchewan just a few years ago, when an amendment was introduced to the medical care insurance act of that province which, by insuring the services of physicians, effectively denied physicians the opportunity to practise medicine properly. This is what the fight was all about; and if the minister does not know this yet, I think it is about time he looked into the situation a little more carefully, before making statements to the house.
[DOT] (7:20 p.m.)
I say at the outset, Mr. Chairman, that despite this mistake-and I hope it is that, which has been made by the Minister of National Health and Welfare-I concur wholeheartedly with the suggestion implicit in the resolution of federal contributions to help pay part of the costs of medical services incurred by provinces pursuant to any provincial medicare program.
I note, coming to another point, that there is nothing in this resolution which indicates whether or not there has been any change in the attitude of the government-and I have heard various views on this tonight-toward the four provisos that the minister previously indicated would be included in the medical care legislation. That change in attitude has to do with the provinces themselves. It is of the utmost importance, Mr. Chairman, to every province in Canada to know exactly the stand of the Canadian government as to which province will or will not be able to

July 12, 1966
Health and Welfare
participate in this shared cost program. Despite what the minister says, this is ambiguous.
My own province oi Saskatchewan has ol course met these four provisos, and we will welcome any additional moneys from the federal government. I am sure that that will allow the government to do away with the direct tax it presently has, and make this program free-if one puts those words in parenthesis-to the people of Saskatchewan.
While we are not so naive as to believe that medical care will be free, as suggested, we think that the distribution costs will be made on a more equitable basis, since it seems that the federal government's share of the cost can allow the Saskatchewan government to eliminate the direct tax it now imposes. I believe that this direct tax, which is easily paid by those in a position to do so, is not so easily paid by some who are neither within the ambit of social aid assistance, nor high enough on the income scale to permit payment of this tax without hardship.
Much has been said, however, by the minister and by members of the other parties as to what effect provision of medical care on a universally available basis will have on the health standards of Canadians. Much has been said about the supposed opposition of Canada's medical profession to the proposed implementation of universal medical care. I should like to discuss both these statements in some detail and clear up, if at all possible, many of the misunderstandings which have arisen regarding the stand of the medical profession.
Page 2, volume 2 of the Royal Commission on Health Services contains a quotation from the Canadian Medical Association brief submitted to the Royal Commission on Health Services in May, 1962. In this brief the C.N.A. said:
-insurance to prepay the costs of medical services should be available to all regardless of age, state of health or financial status.
Commenting on this statement the royal commission said, on the same page:
-it is clear that this policy intends that every Canadian will have or will be entitled to have prepaid coverage enabling each and every one to seek the services of a physician and to receive the services which in his physician's judgment are required.
I point out to the minister that you do not insure services, and I draw his attention to the famous statement made by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam in regard to insuring services when he was asked that question

during the medical care crisis in his province. He said that you cannot insure physicians' services because, as he said: "You can no more lead a horse to water and make it drink than you can take a doctor and make him practise medicine." Despite the fact that he had to eat those words later, I think the meaning is clear to us today.
It seems clear to me that this statement, which is supported by an overwhelming majority of Canadian doctors, is unequivocal and clearly indicates support for a program of prepaid medical care for every person in Canada. It should be noted that this brief was submitted to the royal commission prior to the culmination of the difficulties in Saskatchewan in July of 1962 when despite what is said by certain individuals and politicians, the battle was joined there, not because of opposition to prepaid medical care but because of opposition to what we sincerely believed was an attempt by a provincial government to control the medical profession. I know that there are those who take issue with me in this regard, and they are entitled to their interpretation. I think, on the other hand, conversely, that I too am entitled to my views on this matter.
You may wonder, Mr. Chairman, what application these remarks have to the resolution before the house, but I believe that it is essential to the understanding and application of the resolution that there be a clear knowledge of what pitfalls and stumbling blocks must be avoided by the government in order to bring in the proposed legislation in an atmosphere of reasoned understanding.
As I have said, many attempts have been made to claim that the doctors were opposed to prepaid medical care. I have heard on public platforms and in the news media deliberate distortions which indicated that doctors were opposed to this because the income tax would find out how much money they were making, or that they would make less money under a medical care scheme. I have even heard a prominent former member of this house claim that the doctors were afraid of prepaid medical care because the standard of medicine was so low in this country, and we did not want anybody else to find out about it.
What are the facts? I should like to refer briefly not to what socialist governments, not to what governments bent on welfare statism have done, but to what individuals and doctors have done to bring about programs of prepaid medical care.
July 12, 1966



In 1929 the medical profession pioneered in Saskatchewan the free treatment of tuberculosis. Sanitoriums were set up under a system of private enterprise, with the municipalities supporting the scheme on a per capita basis. In 1931 the profession co-operated with the government, establishing diagnostic and therapeutic cancer clinics available to all at a modest fee. This fee was eliminated by the way under the Liberal government of Saskatchewan prior to the socialists gaining power in 1944.
For many years our country areas were serviced by a local tax-supported municipal scheme. This was pioneered by a citizen of Saskatchewan, Mr. Matthew Anderson, reeve of the municipality of McKillop, in Bulyea, and as a result of his singlehanded action and laudable persistence, an act respecting medical and hospital services in municipalities was assented to in the Legislature of Saskatchewan on April 1, 1939. It may be of interest to some of my friends on the left to know that this included hospital care, medical care and necessary medicines and appliances furnished upon prescription. It seems to me that no mention is ever made by those of socialistic persuasion of the very effective and useful efforts of this private citizen, who operated in a milieu of private enterprise to see that the rural areas were very well served indeed.
A great need still remained in our cities and large towns. To fill this gap the medical profession of Saskatchewan between 1934 and 1938 organized several voluntary non-profit prepaid medical care plans. Much was said during the medicare struggle to the effect that these doctor-sponsored plans were making a great deal of money at the expense of the people of Saskatchewan, despite the fact that they were incorporated under the cooperative assistance act of Saskatchewan, were completely non-profit, and were owned completely by those who took out membership in them.
Despite what we had in this field, there were still gaps in medical care, particularly with those low-income groups who did not qualify for social aid and still could not afford the low premiums of the voluntary plans. So it was that in 1941 the Saskatchewan College of Physicians and Surgeons, in co-operation with the government of the day, set up a continuing committee to consider a universally available province-wide health insurance scheme. Despite these overtures by the medical profession, nothing was done, and
Health and Welfare
in 1944 the C.C.F. government came into power in Saskatchewan. The medical profession offered its co-operation to this government and as a result, in 1944, medical coverage for old age pensioners, the blind, and indigent widows with families was established.
[DOT] (7:30 p.m.)
At the outset this plan was subsidized up to 60 per cent by the medical profession. Hospitalization in that province is a matter of record. Our profession continued to press for an extension of the proposed health insurance scheme. Many meetings were held with the minister of health and with the premier of the province, now the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam; but it was not until 1950, if I remember correctly, that he gave up his cabinet post and Hon. T. J. Bentley took over as minister of health. Following this, the college received a letter stating that no further discussions or negotiations would be held at that time. That was the situation in Saskatchewan. We never hear this from the other side of the fence at all.
We felt they were waiting to find-if I may use this word; it appears in the resolution before us-an expedient time to introduce a bill into the Saskatchewan legislature. I do not know how many hon. members know what "expedient" means, but I took the trouble to look it up. Here, in the Concise Oxford Dictionary, it says "politic rather than just". I leave this to the imaginations of hon. members.
The hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam said the reason they did not bring in a program was that they did not have the money. I accept this view; it is perhaps correct. But this does seem to fly in the face of the contention expressed today by members in that corner of the house that medical care really does not cost any more money, since you are merely taking the amount presently being spent and distributing it among the whole citizenry, giving more equitable coverage.
However, our voluntary plans went on. They covered almost 40 per cent of our population. Taking this percentage along with municipal coverage, coverage of old age pensioners, the blind, widows, mothers' allowances, workmen's compensation, cancer clinics and so on, only 10 per cent of our population had no assistance with their medical bills.
That is interesting, I would think. What happened next? Well, into this improbable

July 12. 1966
Health and Welfare
situation, medicare was introduced. I shall not take the time of the committee now by telling the long and dolorous story of what happened over the next few years. Certainly the lack of communication between the medical profession and the government of Saskatchewan was very like the failure of communication surrounding the "Seven Days" crisis within the C.B.C. Nobody seemed able to get together with anybody else, and I think the reasons were the same as those which the hon. member for York East mentioned the other day when he was discussing the "Seven Days" affair-it was management, rather than the other group, which was causing the trouble.
Eventually a commission under Dr. W. P. Thompson was set up to study not only the question of a medical care plan as originally proposed, but the entire health needs of the province of Saskatchewan. The commission continued its hearings on into 1961. A campaign was mounted against the doctors, and people were made to believe they were against a medical care scheme. The government was re-elected. Hon. members know the rest of the story.
But it was in 1961 that the Canadian Medical Association approached the then prime minister of Canada, the present Leader of the Opposition, and urged him to set up a Royal Commission on Health Services. This has been said before, but it is worthy of repetition: It is as a result of this commission on health services under the chairmanship of Mr. Justice Emmett Hall that the present resolution is before us today.
I have mentioned previously the effect of insuring physicians' services and the iniquitous type of legislation which was brought in in Saskatchewan. A large number of doctors withdrew their services. We did not go on strike. If we did, the Labour members who sit on my left may wonder how we could have a strike and continue to work.
Nevertheless, medical care continues in Saskatchewan. I am not claiming that all the blame was on one side. Most of it was, but not all of it. The doctors themselves, under great emotion, said and did things which they should not have done; but I still believe, and they still believe, that our stand was basically a correct one and I should not like to see a repetition of these tragic events in any other area of Canada.
As a result of this attempt to insure the services of physicians, much was said about

the deterioration of medical care under a medical care scheme. The Hall Commission and the present Minister of National Health and Welfare seem to feel that implementation of a medical care plan will not affect the quality of care, nor will it be a burden on the present facilities, and indeed the Hall Commission on page 9, volume 2, of its report, states as follows:
We can hope therefore that the introduction of universal insurance in Canada will reduce our present losses to the United States, and will result in Canada becoming self-sufficient as the new medical schools are established and existing schools expanded.
I mentioned earlier what happened in Saskatchewan. I think it is worth mentioning again, however briefly-I was thinking of the medical school at the University of Saskatchewan-that instead of producing more graduates, we produced fewer. It should be remembered by all hon. members of the committee that what we are adopting by this resolution is largely the result of an excellent study that took place as a result of the initiative of the former Conservative government. The report that emerged from the Royal Commission on Health Services, better known as the Hall report, charted the course of comprehensive health care which, over the next few years, will ensure that Canada has one of the most progressive programs to take care of all her citizens of any country in the world.
It is not necessary to reiterate many of the statements made tonight and this afternoon. We are concerned about this health problem because, as has been indicated by several speakers, it is one of the major problems that Canada has had to face. The previous speaker mentioned the high cost of illness, amounting to between one billion and two billion dollars per annum. He also referred to the tremendous loss in terms of man days, amounting to $100 million per year. I merely repeat his observations at this time to underline the fact that we are dealing with a most important matter.
The amazing thing about this program is that it has taken years to develop. The minister in introducing his resolution took bows on behalf of his party for its initiative. He has been in this house about the same length of time as I have, and I am sure he will agree that activity in this field in the early 1950's was conspicuous by its absence. The minister now wants to ensure that we have a comprehensive health insurance program on the statute books by July 1, 1967, so the government can take all the credit derived therefrom. We certainly agree that the principle as outlined by the minister in his statement should be implemented as

I am merely raising this point to indicate to the minister that while the target date of July 1 is a worthy and laudable objective, I hope he will continue his consultation with

July 12. 1966

the provinces so that the scheme contemplated by the federal government-we have not yet seen the bill so we do not know what the details might be; our discussion is preliminary to the introduction of the legislation-to be inaugurated next year will be carried out with a minimum of friction. I think it would be disastrous for social legislation of this kind if we were to enter into a period of provincial-federal bickering which has marked so much of the progress of the present Liberal administration in Ottawa during the past three years.
Here is a place where co-operative federalism, or consultative federalism might be used to the maximum advantage in order to ensure that the conflicting viewpoints of the provinces might be reconciled with the co-ordinating function of the federal government in so far as it is humanly possible to do so. While Manitoba has always taken a reasonable viewpoint in these matters-and I think that Manitoba, in the federal scheme of things, has established a reputation for being reasonable and moderate in all things-I believe the minister will agree that the position of the province of Alberta is a little more difficult and is something with which he will have to come to grips before the program can be implemented.
I am not going to deal with the principles that have been enunciated by the government in this regard, but I should like to make a few suggestions, which perhaps have already been incorporated in the bill to come before the house. It seems to me that if we are to come to grips with the problem of medicare on a comprehensive basis, we have to deal with three fundamental aspects of this question, the preventive, the therapeutic and the restorative. In medicine as well as in any other field of human activity, an ounce of prevention is better than a pound of cure. I think the minister will agree that so far as health services are concerned the educational function is the basic function in providing an adequate basis for the prevention of illness and disease. This is the priority that the government of Manitoba has constantly repeated in its representations on this matter.
When we come to the therapeutic aspect we must take into consideration that adequate therapy involves the treatment of the whole patient. I am not an expert or authority on these matters-we have already had some well qualified medical practitioners participating in this discussion-but I noticed a

little cartoon in the week end newspaper which pointed out one of the difficulties of the practice of medicine at the present time. The cartoon depicted a group of doctors surrounding a patient, and one doctor was saying to the others, "Do you know, that was a very difficult situation. I was almost one half inch out of the area of my specialization." In other words, the science of medicine, the science of medical therapy has advanced to such a state of specialization today that sometimes we fail to take into consideration the fact, and it is a basic fact, that in any illness or disease the whole person is involved.
This brings me, Mr. Chairman, to an important aspect of illness which is not covered in any of the existing health schemes operating in any of the provinces, and that is an adequate approach to the problems of mental illness. It is becoming increasingly recognized by the authorities in the field that when a person is ill, the whole person is suffering from the illness, and the psychosomatic branch of medical science is only now emerging as perhaps one of the encouraging new developments in the field. Mr. Justice Hall in his excellent report makes a strong bid for the inclusion of adequate mental health care in any program of health insurance that will be brought before this parliament. He said there must be the removal of all discrimination in the distinctions made between physical and mental illness.
I trust that in the proposals to be brought forward by the minister and the government adequate consideration will be given to this fundamental aspect of therapy, even though it cannot be implemented on a comprehensive basis at this stage because the final initiative, as I have indicated, will rest with the provincial governments. I know several provincial governments are interested in this aspect and I trust that the legislation will make it possible for the provinces which are ready to move forward to seize the initiative in this regard.

There is just one other point which I should like to make. I do not want to speak at length because many of the points have already been covered and repetition at this stage should be avoided at all costs. However I do want to repeat that the Royal Commission on Health Services in outlining the health charter for this nation emphasized, as many of the provincial governments and many speakers in this debate have done, the
July 12, 1966

necessity for taking priorities into consideration. We are living in a day and age of specialization, and if we are going to have a co-ordinated program-and the essential function of the federal government is that of co-ordination-we must provide, as the Hall Royal Commission has pointed out, for a health planning council so that we can avoid the hit or miss approach to the problem which has existed hitherto.
We must also expand the existing medical resources council which could perhaps be described as a health sciences resources council. All sorts of new disciplines have emerged in recent years in the field of health care.
The role of the social scientist has become increasingly important as has the role of the social worker. I wonder how many hospitals today are adequately equipped with social scientists, psychologists, sociologists and social workers so that the whole person and his problem can come under treatment? I would venture to say there are very few hospitals adequately staffed in this way. The advent of our national health program will immensely aggravate the problem. The program will create the need for proper hospital planning, specially trained architects and administrators to handle the specialized problems arising in modern hospital care, as well as statisticians to compile the data necessary in order to diagnose the problem adequately and then to treat it.
We heartily endorse this scheme. I also wish to express my admiration for the government's belief that this program can be launched successfully by July 1 of 1967. Many long years have been wasted. I hope, Mr. Chairman, that this is not a piece of legislation put forward in the spirit of the 60 days of decision. I am sure the minister appreciates the fact that before the program that he contemplates and that is recommended by the Royal Commission is initiated, much more careful consideration and consultation with the provinces in whose hands rests the initiative will be necessary.

It is good to hear these hon. members who have been born since that day rejoicing in the fact that it has taken the Liberal party only 47 years to implement the plan that was drafted in 1919. It is good for the people of Canada that at last some action is being taken on this issue.
I may also say Mr. Chairman, that it is very interesting for us to hear our speeches coming back to us from the minister. It was really a delight this afternoon to hear all the arguments that we have used over the years to try to get the Liberals to move, now being used by the minister. He told us about the

July 12, 1966
Health and Welfare
social responsibility that rests upon Canada to provide for the health of our people. He told us that it would make good economic sense. We cannot object to these arguments because they are the arguments we have been using in this chamber for all the decades during which we have been here.
The minister also drew to our attention the fact that private insurance schemes fail to provide complete coverage for the people of Canada. He gave figures which showed that for all the good that might be said by some hon. members about private schemes, in the end there has to be a public scheme if all the people of Canada are to be covered. As I said, we are glad to hear the speeches we have made over the decades being pronounced in this house today by a minister of the crown advocating this legislation.
[DOT] (8:30 p.m.)
We have also heard another very important argument which we have used over the years, namely that a health insurance program does not involve an expenditure of new money to any great extent. What a health insurance program does is to redistribute the cost of medical care. This afternoon the minister gave us actual figures. He said that under the legislation it is anticipated that $680 million will be spent on medical care in the first year in which the plan was in effect. He pointed out, however, that even without this legislation we are spending $600 million for comparable services. After all, therefore, we are simply adding a total of $80 million to the amount of money the Canadian people are spending but we are distributing the cost by this legislation so that it will be borne by the people of Canada according to their ability to pay, but health care will go to the people of Canada according to their need.
This is a good. This is a great day. It is wonderful to have been alive in 1919 when medicare was proposed by the Liberals. It is wonderful still to be alive when it is put into effect 47 years later. I see the minister has borrowed the book and is looking it up. It is on page 205 of the report of the Liberal convention which met in Ottawa in August, 1919.

speechtext:
You are more than welcome. As I was about to say, I wish to echo for a moment the question put by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam this afternoon. It is good to know we are going to get this legislation; but when, is still a question that this house must face. I want to say, as urgently as I can, that I think the House of Commons should go all the way with this legislation before it rises for a summer recess. I think the bill should be passed through all stages.
The Minister of National Health and Welfare suggested that at least he would like to go as far as second reading. This is almost all the way; it would be approval in principle by the House of Commons. I want to say that in view of the kind of discussion that has taken place here today, in view of the differences of opinion that exist, I think the country has a right to know where parliament stands. I do not see how the provinces in this country can make their plans during the summer months on the basis of the debate that has taken place today. The provinces can make their plans only after the legislation has been passed, or certainly has had second reading, so that approval in principle is clear.
I want to suggest to the members of this of the whole committee that in asking the government to go all the way with this legislation we are not asking for something new. Hon. members know that I have been on my feet on orders of the day, or on "late shows", as often as I could during this session to try to get a commitment out of the government. We got a commitment. On three or four occasions the Prime Minister and the Minister of National Health and Welfare indicated it was the desire of the government to deal in full with this medicare legislation before a summer recess. References can be found in Hansard for June 1, June 22, and in several other places. I have the various clippings from Hansard on my desk, as a matter of fact.
I submit, Mr. Chairman, that if we do not get the legislation through at this time or at least get it approved in principle on second reading, the chances are slim of medicare being in effect on July 1, 1967. If this measure is not considered until the fall, I suggest that the debate we have had here today indicates the second reading debate will be a long one. Before you know it, it will be

July 12, 1966

Christmas and the provinces will not be in a position to pass complementary legislation. The suggestion that the legislation should go to a committee for study is a plausible one. However, Mr. Chairman, as a result of the studies that have been given to this matter in the last half century, surely we are in a position to act. I think of the various reports we have had during the years, such as the Heagerty report, the Marsh report, and so on. I think of all the work that went into the preparation of the green books that were presented to the federal-provincial conference in 1945. I think of an actual bill that was laid on the table of this house in 1944 or 1945 by Hon. Ian Mackenzie, then minister of pensions and national health.
All of these studies have been updated by the studies into health grants and hospitalization, as well as many departmental studies. We took this matter up in the estimates committee a few years ago and a very exhaustive study of it was conducted by the members of this house. Now we have had the Hall report, and members in all parts of the house agree that this was a tremendous study. There have been federal-provincial conferences galore, and I suggest that basically parliament is in a position to make up its mind on this question. I hope we will do it now so that the target date of our 100th birthday can be met with respect to this important question.
I said that we are in full support of this legislation. Any suggestions or criticisms that we might make would be with respect to the details. There are one or two to which I want to refer briefly. I note that the wording the Prime Minister used last July regarding the scope of the services to be covered seemed to me to be a little broader than the wording used today by the minister. Last July the Prime Minister talked in terms of all the services that might be required. The minister today talked in terms of physicians' services of all kinds. Then, he said, he hoped, in the not too distant future, he will be in a position to enlarge on these services.
This strikes me as imposing a limitation, at least in spirit, that was not contained in the announcement the Prime Minister made last July. I should like to suggest this to the Minister of National Health and Welfare. He had a great deal to say during the debate on the Canada Assistance Plan about the fact that there is no ceiling on the assistance or the welfare services in which the federal government will participate. I suggest that he
Health and Welfare
should apply the same principle to this legislation. If a province wants to enlarge the range of insured services, the federal government should agree to that and should place no limitation on it, any more than it does on the assistance or the welfare services set out in the Canada Assistance Plan. I remind the minister also that on May 17 of this year, as recorded in Hansard at page 5213, he announced the government's decision to let medicare come into effect in any province that agreed to it without waiting for the majority of all provinces. We immediately approved of that stand, and we still approve of that position. It seems to me that consistent with that position, namely that a province that wants to come in can do so without waiting for the others, is the further position that if a province or two or three provinces want to go further than some of the others in the services that are to be insured, the federal government should go along with that position. We will develop this idea when we go into committee on the bill.
There is one other point that I think we will want to look at rather closely when we are considering the bill, and that is with respect to what is known as the third criterion. I refer to the one having to do with plans being provincially administered. Here, again, I detected a slight difference between the wording of last July and the wording of today. I was only slightly concerned when the minister spoke, but I was really quite exercised when the hon. member for Coast-Capilano spoke because he seemed to see in this wording a possibility of private carriers being included in the plan. I realize that the hon. member for Coast-Capilano does not speak for the government, but at least he has posed a question with which we will want to deal when we go into committee.
[DOT] (8:40 p.m.)
The time for this debate is limited and we are limited to 20 minutes, so I shall cut my remarks short. There are in fact just two more things I want to say, and I can say them briefly. In the course of this debate those who have been critical of this legislation have trotted out the word "priorities". They spoke about two other things that should come first. Last year when we were debating the Canada Pension Plan we had this same argument. People then were saying: We must establish priorities. Education and health were regarded by some speakers as matters that had priority over the Canada Pension Plan. Today, because we are dealing

July 12, 1966
Health and Welfare
with health, the people who were talking in this way are saying that education and pensions should take priority over health. I suppose if we had a bill to provide massive sums of money for education those same people would be saying that health and social security should have priority over education.
It seems to me, in a country that has a gross national product of $55 billion, in a country that has the affluence and the prospects of this country, that we do not need to talk about one or the other of these things. We have the money to provide social security, education, and health. Those who talk about priorities, as I see it, are attempting to slow down our work in this important field. I urge that we have the capacity to go along with all these important aspects of social welfare, and I hope that we shall do so without the kind of delay that we have had from the party opposite, which has taken 47 years to implement the three most important planks in its 1919 platform.
The other point I should like to make relates to the complaints that some people have made about the payments that will have to be made for medicare, even though it is clear that there will be no premium at the federal level, and even though it is clear that, for the most part, our medical services will be paid for out of general revenue. The point was made by an hon. member that this involves taxes, and that our people do not like taxes of any sort.
I know it is an old cliche, and it is an adage that everybody does not agree with, but I think it is true that taxes are the price we pay for civilization. I suggest if we must pay taxes for civilization, one of the aspects of civilization that is most worth paying for is the good health of our people. I urge that we do not keep finding these excuses for a slow-down with respect to this legislation, but that we recognize, as was said the other day by my leader, and as was subsequently said by others, that the best thing we can do to celebrate our one hundredth birthday, on July 1, 1967, is to have medicare in effect.
I urge therefore, Mr. Chairman, that this committee of the whole and this House of Commons act on this legislation in the light of its importance, that we get this resolution through, and that we proceed with the bill before we think of going home for a summer recess.

I could not help noting that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre kept referring to the Liberal platform policy

which had been announced back in 1919. It seems to me, ever since I have been here, since 1962, that that has been the permanent line adopted by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. I would point out to him how tedious it is to hear the same line day in and day out, and how refreshing it would be to hear something novel and original.
I think it will be well, before the hon. member talks about how long it has taken some parties to implement their policies, to remember that the leader of his party for almost 20 years was premier of Saskatchewan, before he brought in medicare legislation in the early 1960's. It would be well for the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre to bear that in mind before talking of how long it has taken other parties to implement their programs. I do not think it is pertinent to discuss what some political parties might have done or said 30 or 40 years ago. I think the point to remember is that now we have legislation before us, and that we should get on with it and put it into effect.
That brings me logically to the position taken by the official opposition. It seems that they would prefer to deal with the initial stages of the legislation now, and then deal with the remainder of it, namely, second reading, if I am stating their position correctly, later. I find this a very difficult position to comprehend, especially when one looks at the stages that this program has gone through in the last three years, to wind up in the resolution before us today.
We had the royal commission-and a good commission it was-set up by the Conservative government between 1958 and 1962. That commission reported two and a half years ago, and it came out with its second volume less than two years ago. Following the publication of these two reports-actually it would be more accurate to say that the second volume came out one and a half years ago-the government launched an intensive study of its recommendations. After that the government took the initiative and put forward proposals at a federal-provincial conference in July, one year ago. These were the proposals setting down the four criteria which have been referred to frequently today.
That shows progress, I would say, that no one should be ashamed of. These reports had to be studied, and they were studied intensely. Federal-provincial conferences were called, and the first one of real significance was over one year ago when the four criteria were laid down which are contained in the
July 12, 1966



bill we have coming before us, and which have been submitted in this resolution.
There is nothing novel about the matter. Members of this house have been aware of this legislation, and of its nature, for over one year. We all have been aware of the royal commission report for well over two years. Why it should take any further mulling over, or why it should need any further time for discussion over the recess is hard to understand.
I would think in view of the royal commission's findings, in view of the ample material there available for all to study, in view of the fact that the principal ingredients of this resolution were laid before a federal-provincial conference over a year ago-ingredients which have changed hardly at all and which are contained in this resolution, and in this proposed legislation-we should be able to complete this legislation within a day or two. I would urge that that course of action be adopted. We should then have done something which we could be proud of accomplishing prior to recess.
I think now, Mr. Chairman, it would be appropriate for me to deal with some of the principal objections taken to this legislation. The objection you often hear, although it has not been referred to too much in this house today, is the objection to there being any target date. It has been suggested that setting a target date is unnecessary and unrealistic. With this I do not agree. Without target date discussions can drift, and it can be years before any progress is made.
Another criticism that is most often repeated concerns the universality of application of these proposals, and of the compulsory element that flows from such application. As has been mentioned, the government put forward four basic principles which it felt were prerequisite to the federal government sharing the cost. It has been argued in some quarters that one or more of these criteria should be deleted. One of the principal criteria to which objection has been made is that provincial schemes should be universal in coverage. Opponents of medicare argue that this principle is repugnant to a free society-that it involves compulsion and is not in keeping with a democratic society.

speechtext: I suggest that universality is an essential ingredient of any real medicare program. Elementary education, for example, is now universal-compulsory, if you like-as are vaccination and pasteurization. Amother objection one hears, and it has been raised by some medical associations, is that medicare will turn medical practitioners into civil servants. I do not believe this is so. A further objection-I heard it in this committee today-is that medicare will impose an intolerable burden on the economy, one which Canada is not ready to assume. I do not think that either the facts or the experiences of other nations bear this out.
A further criticism, and one which is related to the financial argument, is that medicare at this time is politically motivated and that it has been placed improperly on the list of priorities to the prejudice of other measures which are badly needed. Education is usually mentioned as a public need which has been forced to take second place to medicare.
The primary objection which seems to be worthy of mention is that medicare as presently envisaged by the federal government will severely prejudice the quality of medical services available to Canadians. This is an objection which the hon. member for Simcoe East stressed this afternoon. While I could not agree with many of his observations I felt his was a speech with real content, one which included many worthwhile suggestions.
I have outlined the principal objections here to the medicare proposals. I should like to deal particularly with the arguments of

July 12, 1966
Health and Welfare
those who object to universality. They feel it compromises freedom of choice-that it compels people to participate in the plan and is foreign to the tenets of democracy.
Surely it is necessary to introduce the principle of universality in any program which so closely affects the health and life of all Canadians. The voluntary approach would never result in everyone being covered. This is a proven fact. I should like to refer hon. members to some figures on this aspect of the subject. The very group which would not be covered by voluntary plans is often the group which fails to receive adequate and, all too often, essential medical care. Universality may lessen an individual's freedom from coercion, but for many, total freedom is enhanced; for many it is the key to the enjoyment of such fundamental rights as freedom from want and freedom from fear.
We talk of equal opportunity. How can we achieve this lofty goal when there are many who for lack of means do not receive adequate health care? How are these people physically able to participate fully in, and contribute to, society? How can they share in the opportunities afforded their more fortunate compatriots?

talking of those goods produced and distributed on the basis of the open market system, a system where the voluntary element is circumscribed only by the dictates of price. We are talking of something much more than services which someone provides because he can turn a profit. We are dealing with services where, for a variety of cogent reasons, such considerations do not apply.
To raise the criticism of lack of choice and, at the same time, to limit it to medical services-one area in the whole health services field-is quite incomprehensible. If this criticism has any validity, should it not be equally applicable to the whole spectrum of health services?
By insisting on universality the federal government has gone a long way toward ensuring that Canadians will pay the most reasonable rates for medical coverage. The risk will be spread among all the people. In this connection I should like to refer to a comparison of rates under different schemes.
Many critics of medicare advocate that coverage be provided by private insurance companies and that these companies be subsidized to provide coverage for those unable to pay their own way. They suggest that private companies could provide this service at a fraction of the cost of the federal proposal. The facts do not bear out this contention.
Figures show that private plans pay out considerably less revenue on claims than do public sponsored plans. The Hall Royal Commission figures show that retained moneys, that is, money not paid out in claims, for private plans range from 38 per cent to a low of 18.5 per cent for a prepaid plan. This covers direct administrative costs, acquisition of new members, commissions, taxes, reserves and profits. In Saskatchewan on the other hand the retention ratio, free of reserves and profits, was only 6.39 per cent in 1963 and 5.81 per cent in 1964. From this comparison it can be seen that there will be a heavy obligation on provincial administrations to have these plans publicly administered.
Another objection in the summary of criticisms is the fact that doctors would now be relegated to the role of civil servants. Such an allegation is set out in a draft letter that the Ontario Medical Association sent to doctors throughout the province, asking them to 23033-4811
Health and Welfare
sign it and send it their patients. I quote one paragraph from that letter:

Referring to the doctor who it is proposed should send out the letter.
-am deeply concerned about Mr. Pearson's proposal because a compulsory, government operated medicare plan could adversely affect our relationship. I would become virtually an employee of the government, and would not be free to care for you and your family in the same way I have done in the past.
Such an allegation is simply not correct. It presupposes that the doctor will not be able to choose his patients; that the patient will not be able to choose his or her physician; that the doctor will not be free to practise where he wishes; that the doctor's fees will be arbitrarily set and that doctors will not have the choice to practise in or out of any government sponsored program. These are the faulty assumptions inherent in the draft letter.
Any provincial scheme can be implemented and qualify within the four criteria and, at the same time, guarantee the preservation of all the above rights, rights which are repugnant to any employee-employer relationship. It has not been suggested by anyone at the federal or provincial level that the doctors would not have the freedom of choice of patient, or the patient freedom of choice of doctor. It has not been suggested that the method of payment to the doctor would be on other than a fee for service basis.
It has not been suggested by anyone that there be any regulations governing where a doctor can carry on his practice. In fact, it has been suggested in the Hall Commission report that the fee schedule would be determined through consultation between the government and the recognized associations representing the medical professionals. How then can it be said that the doctor becomes a government employee or civil servant? How then can it be said that the government is interfering with the doctor-patient relationship?

Mr. Chairman, during the course of his introductory remarks this afternoon the minister made a request which the committee, I am quite sure, will comply with, that the proposal he has submitted will receive the constructive and conscientious attention of the house. I trust therefore that if the attention that members give to his proposal, and to the statement he made this afternoon, gives rise in turn to some difference of opinion and criticism, he and the government will give those contrary opinions and those criticisms the same degree and kind of attention that the minister bespoke for his own proposal.
I am quite sure that a statement which would receive universal acceptance is that a proposal that prepaid medical services be available to all Canadians is a valid and desirable objective, and a proper objective for government to seek to accomplish. But I suggest to you, Mr. Chairman, that we as members of parliament cannot be carried away by a mere statement of objective and that we are still entitled, and indeed required to examine any specific proposal laid before us by the government, in this and any other field, in the light of certain criteria.
The two criteria which I suggest apply most particularly and forcefully here, and which we are bound to bring to bear upon examination of this proposal are these: First, how does the proposal meet the test of economic realism? How does it fit in with any realistic assessment of the priorities-and I make no apology for using that word-to be allotted to government objectives and expenditures? I hope the government will not take the position that it must rush blindly after all objectives that occur to it, without trying to assign some priorities among them.
And second, how does the proposal in question meet the test of constitutional propriety? I use the reference to the constitution here not from the sense or point of view of strict legal application-the question of whether or not the legislation is ultra vires or inter vires-but rather use the words constitutional propriety in the sense of the proper relationship between the two levels of government in Canada, and applying to the proposed activities of the federal government the test of whether or not they involve an unjustifiable intrusion by it into a field which properly belongs to another level of government.
[The Deputy Chairman.]
I suggest most strongly, Mr. Chairman, that on the basis of an examination of the government's previous announcements in connection with its medicare program, and an analysis of the minister's statement this afternoon, the proposal he has placed before this committee, and will place before the house, has very serious deficiencies with respect to both the criteria that I have suggested should be applied.
Looking first at the matter of the economic realism of the proposal, I suggest to you, Mr. Chairman, and to members of the committee, that what is involved here, when a scheme such as the minister has in mind is in full flower, will present a major distortion of the economy and of any realistic scheme of priorities.
[DOT] (9:10 p.m.)
Mr. Chairman, all welfare schemes and projects are desirable; of course they are. Anything that will contribute to the betterment of our people, to the better care of our health, to our needs in old age, or any other aspect of our lives as Canadians, is desirable. But it seems to me that as a growing, developing young country we must assign priorities to the problems which confront us. We must bear in mind that the federal government is not responsible for all aspects of Canadian life or all the welfare of Canadians. Nor are the resources available to the government without limit; and therefore it is prudent and proper in the interest of Canadians to insist that the federal government bring a measure of judgment to bear with regard to what its programs will be and on what basis it intends to carry them out, as well as the priority assigned to them.
At the moment, on the basis of proposals and commitments made by the government, we are faced with a vast increase in commitments for expenditures in respect of security measures. In respect of the Canada Pension Plan-the cost of which I have yet to see authoritatively stated-the estimated cost is at least $600 million per annum. We are apparently about to be committed to a medicare plan which at its inception, on the basis of the statement made by the minister this afternoon, will cost $340 million per annum out of the federal treasury. Recently we have had the Bladen report on the needs of education in Canada, much of which has been approved in principle and in respect of which a commitment in principle has been given by the Prime Minister. If implemented in toto its cost can reach an astronomical amount; the
July 12, 1966

commitments given will probably amount to some $500 million per annum out of the federal treasury.
So that on the basis of just those three
commitments, in what I might describe generally as the field of welfare, at least $1,500 million-and I suggest closer to $2 million per annum-more has been committed to be raised by federal taxes and paid out of the federal treasury, than was the case just 18 months ago.
And that is in these three areas alone,
leaving aside other real responsibilities of the federal government in such important and vital areas as our responsibility in the field of anti-pollution and de-pollution of our water resources. These increased costs are on the basis of present estimates and I suggest, Mr. Chairman, that we are entitled on the basis of past experience to assume that the estimated costs are well below what they will in fact turn out to be.
My view is that the government has no right or reason to enter into welfare schemes oblivious of the economic consequences. It has to consider whether there will be sufficient funds available for investment in our economic development and whether we will have to place further reliance on foreign investors for Canadian development.
Is it not a strange situation that here we have a present Minister of Finance and a former minister of finance of this government vying for the leadership of the Liberal party on the basis of the question of foreign investment in Canadian development enterprise. Both of them are committed to allowing this increase in expenditure on this kind of measure, which at the same time is helping to reduce the capital available in the pockets of Canadians for investment and which cannot help but increase our dependence on foreign capital. There is no consistency or logic in the government's position. For a government, some of whose spokesmen are crusading to, "buy back the Canadian economy," this is an odd position indeed.
With respect to the estimated cost of this program alone we already have seen a considerable escalation in the estimate. The government originally estimated the per capita cost at $28 to be shared equally by the federal and provincial governments. I understand it now estimates it at $34, an increase of $6 per head. In other words, within six months the estimated cost of medicare has risen by over 20 per cent.
Health and Welfare
Even the recent figures I believe are overly optimistic. In this connection it is interesting to note the experience of the United Kingdom, with their national health service. Their estimated annual cost of $510 million for the first year turned out to be $1,206 million and has risen steadily to $3,754 million despite the imposition of certain service charges. I suggest that on the basis of that experience, and our own experience, the minister has probably very seriously underestimated both the initial and future annual costs of the medicare program.
I suggest to you, sir, that we should be devoting our energies and our resources to meet the priority needs of the Canadian people and that those priorities really lie in the development programs which would aid in the creation of new jobs. If we concentrated on those, we will eventually reach the position where we would be able to finance even a universal medicare scheme.
I suggest that we take very special consideration of these things and that if we do not the consequences will be disastrous indeed, and if we are to give priority to any form of social measure, I say the priority should be given to education. Even in the field of medicare itself that is where the priority should be given now. In the field of medical assistance we should be providing funds so that we can produce the doctors, teachers and nurses so that we can staff our medicare program.
