On the basis of arguments and considerations I have so far brought forward I submit with all earnestness that the federal government has no right in the first place, and has no reason in logic or in responsibility, to impose this scheme on the provinces as the minister intends to do. I submit, rather, that the approach by the federal government to the plan of prepaid medical services in Canada should be to offer to supplement provincial schemes where there are gaps in the present coverage. Because I believe in matching criticism with constructive proposals I should like to put before the committee and the government at this stage a brief statement of principles upon which I think the federal government's approach to medicare should be based. I will summarize them as follows.
Any plan for prepaid medical coverage to which the federal government contributes should not be on a universal and compulsory basis, but should be based on the following principles:
One, that medical services, at an adequate level, should be available to all Canadians on a prepaid basis.
Two, that this being a field primarily within provincial responsibility, the federal government should not seek to superimpose any national, universal or compulsory scheme on existing provincial schemes.
Three, that the role of the federal government should be to extend to the provinces financial assistance to enable them to establish provincial medicare programs whereby prepaid medical care is available to all citizens at a fixed premium, or cost, but not to compel contributions to or participation in a scheme by those who are now covered adequately, or who are able and prefer to provide medical care for themselves.
Four, that all schemes of prepaid medical care, to qualify for federal assistance, should preserve the voluntary doctor-patient relationship.
Five, that beyond federal participation in such uniform programs to ensure availability of standard coverage, the provinces should be left free to expand or enlarge medical care schemes as they and their voters see fit, while the federal government should concentrate its efforts in the vital fields of encouragement of,

and provision of resources for, training and research in medical, dental, nursing and other related occupations and facilities.
That, in my submission, Mr. Chairman, is a sound and realistic set of principles upon which federal participation in a program of medicare should be based. Such an approach would lead us to offer to the provinces help in a voluntary but universally available plan.
There are other statistics and considerations which argue this way as well. The 1964 survey on voluntary health insurance reported that more than 80 per cent of Canadians were covered then by some form of prepaid medical care. With the Ontario, Alberta and British Columbia plans now in effect, on the basis of some estimates this figure approaches 90 per cent, although I am told that a more realistic estimate is between 86 and 87 per cent. I have seen estimates that 12.8 million Canadians are now covered by adequate prepaid medical care plans.
The government, however, wishes to use a shotgun approach to the problem. In order to provide medical care for the approximately 10 per cent not now covered-and that is the gap we should be concentrating on-the government insists upon a new type of universal plan which will supersede private and corporate plans long in existence. On the basis of the minister's proposal, all private plans must be wiped out and this plan must be publicly administered. Let me ask him and the committee what is going to happen to some of the very adequate and excellent private plans now in existence, under which employees of companies in large numbers are covered? These individuals are covered by medical plans they like, the benefits of which they enjoy. They are perfectly adequate in coverage. Many of these plans are paid for by the employer without any contribution at all by the employee, as the result of agreements arrived at through the years of the process of collective bargaining. These plans are apparently to be wiped out by the minister's proposal, and there will be substituted some sort of universal plan which can only be paid for out of the tax purse, to which these employees will be contributing. This will deprive them of a benefit they have attained as a result of the process of years of collective bargaining.
I suggest the alternative Ontario Medical Services Insurance Plan or the British Columbia plan, which are universally acceptable and under which the provincial governments pay the premium for the lowest income
July 12, 1966

groups, effectively meet the government's objection to a voluntary scheme. They are universally available, and show that the government's fear that the most needy would not participate or benefit can be met without a compulsory program.
Indeed, Mr. Chairman, since the Hall Commission report is being quoted extensively, I think we should remind ourselves of what was said by the commission at page 3 of volume 1 of its report. These are the words used:
The commission believes that the individual's responsibility for his personal health and that of the members of his or her family is paramount to the extent of the individual's capacities.
Surely one can agree with the objective of adequate medical services for all Canadians without endorsing a comprehensive system of compulsory medical insurance.
These are some of the considerations which in my view indicate that the plan of the minister and the government is not economically realistic. As to the other criteria in relation to its constitutional propriety, again I find that there are very serious objections.

In other words, Mr. Chairman, most clearly what is being said is this: Here we are, boys, we have a lot of money in the federal treasury; it is there for you if you will be good and run your medical care programs the way we want you to run them, and not the way you think you should run them. This clearly indicates a heavy-handed use of the club of financial power to force provincial acceptance of federal dictation.
What is the difference between what the minister proposes there, and a proposal that the federal government has money in the treasury and will give it, say, to the province of Manitoba for education if that province will alter its school curriculum and provide for the teaching of French at all levels of their school system? Alternatively, what is the difference between the minister's proposal and the federal government saying to the province of Quebec that it will give that province money from the federal treasury if they will adopt a school system of the kind considered desirable by the people here in Ottawa?
This is nothing more than financial blackmail and it is totally and completely unacceptable.
The federal government makes the boast that what it is doing is co-operative federalism. This is not co-operative federalism: This is dictatorial federalism of the worst sort.

Having listened to the debate this afternoon and evening I can well understand why it has taken nearly 50 years to get the medicare resolution up to the present stage. Before hearing this debate I had no idea that there were so many hon. members in this house who have been talking across the country about the need for medicare and about the need of the sick people; that there have been so many people promising a national scheme of medicare for many years and who have then, on being faced with a good piece of legislation, spoken about the need for education and the need for legislation on this, that or the other thing, and then have mounted a sudden surprise attack stating that this legislation deprives the people of this country of their liberty.
I feel it is time that Canadians saw the way in which so many hon. members in the house are reacting to the legislation now before us and which the government has had the courage and foresight to present to the house. I hope that at this stage the government will not weaken or defer this measure, because I think that if the minister were to leave this matter at the resolution stage, the

summer recess will be used by many hon. members whom we have heard speaking in the house in order to prejudice certain groups of people in their own constituencies against this legislation.
I suggest, Mr. Chairman, that they will await the opportunity of having this matter referred to a committee in order to kill the legislation before it gets any further. I appeal to the government to go ahead with this matter. I can assure the minister that this measure will have the support not only of a sufficient number of us in this house to have it passed but also the support of the people of this country who have been waiting for medicare for such a long time.
We have heard many quotations from the Hall report, and I was very disappointed to hear the hon. member for Kamloops trying to enumerate a few minutes ago all the medical coverage that Canadians have under private schemes at the present time. The Hall report states quite clearly that after more than 35 years of endeavour on the part of voluntary groups and commercial insurance companies, only slightly more than one half of the population of Canada has any degree of voluntary insurance protection, and this for medical services alone. Of this number, the coverage held by nearly three million people is wholly inadequate. Over 7.5 million Canadians have no medical care insurance whatsoever. I think it is time we stopped talking in distorted terms regarding the medical coverage of Canadians.
The Hall report is an exceedingly worthwhile document and its findings have been beyond criticism or dispute. I think that sometimes we are forgetting why this legislation is being introduced at this time. It is simply being introduced because coverage of this kind is urgently needed in Canada. It has been abundantly proven over and over again that not only the small sections of the population about whom we have been hearing tonight, but wide ranges of Canadian citizens simply cannot afford the medical care they need.
We have been hearing about the exceedingly high cost of medicare. Let me remind the house of the cost of illness to our economy at the present time. In 1963, a hundred million man-days of labour have been lost because of illness, which amount to 3.8 per cent of the gross national product of that year, worth over $1.5 billion. If we assume a continued 3.8 per cent loss, the figure for the year 1965
July 12, 1966

reaches at least $2 billion, and that does not include the reduced productivity of those who continue to work while in poor health. Obviously not all of this is preventable, but even if only 10 per cent could be avoided through better health care and greater availability of physicians' services, the gain to our economy would at least be equal to $200 million. I think it is time we began to look at this matter in actual terms instead of bringing forward moss-backed ideas that should have died in the last century.
As I said, we have been considering this measure for approximately 50 years. Other countries of the world are away ahead of us. We have the example of the health plan in New Zealand which has been in existence since the 1930's, and the medicare plans which have been in existence in the Scandinavian countries for a long time. We have had the example of Great Britain and our own province of Saskatchewan. Let me ask these people who are so keenly eager to prove that Great Britain wishes to repudiate its medical plan whether it is not strange that in spite of all the true blue Tory governments which have governed that country since the introduction of the medicare plan, none of those Tory governments has repealed this legislation.

Or
even amended it. They did not dare do it because they knew that if they touched that legislation the common people of Britain would know exactly what to do with them. Let me point out that if the government can get this piece of legislation on the statute books, it will be an enduring memorial to them. It will not be touched by those people who are today making such a fuss from this side of the house. These people who have been complaining about it will never dare to touch it, knowing how needed it is and how popular it will be once the legislation is in effect.
The Hall report made it abundantly clear, too, that another allegation which has been made today is completely wrong. That report has made it abundantly clear that there is no comparison between the cost of administering these private plans and the cost of administering a properly run government medicare scheme. Indeed, the Hall report says that the decisions which Canadians have to make, assuming that they accept the claim of the health insurance industry that it can provide
Health and Welfare
universal coverage, which incidentally the Hall Commission does not accept, is whether they wish to pay $1,020 million for these services in 1971 as administered by the insurance industry, or $837 million for a program administered by governmental agencies.
It has been proven over and over again the public agencies are the ones which can run a medicare scheme more economically. All of us in this corner have been looking forward to getting this legislation before us because we hope, at long last, we are going to be able to turn health care from being a business for profit, as it has been under the private agencies, into a service for the people of Canada. The opponents of this measure say that the cost will go up, and that the Hall Commission estimates have not been high enough. Probably the cost will go up. Costs have gone up for other services and in other industries. Costs are steadily going up these days. I point this out, that if the cost of a public medicare scheme goes up, the cost for private schemes under private agencies will go up too. People who are today without medical service coverage will be just that much worse off than they were. I think there is no argument in saying that costs will go up.
There have been a number of pieces of evidence given concerning the benefits to the people of a publicly administered medicare scheme. I want to give just one single bit of evidence which was given to those of us who were in Vancouver attending the national conference of social workers a week or two ago. Professor Titmuss of the London School of Economics was referring to the benefits that had come to the British people as a result of the health services. He gave this illustration, that the incidence of cataract in people over 70 has declined by 30 per cent in 12 years in Great Britain. This is a disease that is tremendously prevalent among older people.
May I give one other example of what is happening? This may impress hon. members even more. The incidence of blindness is down 25 per cent in Great Britain over the last ten years.

I am saying that a reputable person, Professor Titmuss, one of the best known authorities in Great Britain on social welfare measures, made the statement that during the last 12 years, during which time medicare was in force in Britain, one of the greatest triumphs had been the reduction of blindness by 25 per cent. They were able to get treatment for cataract on a large scale.
Let me point out that one of the difficulties we have encountered in Canada has been the fact that the business of providing medical services has been a private industry. The doctors, whether they wanted to or not, have not been in the position to give service to those who most needed it, the people in the lower income group. The hon. member who just asked me the question was this afternoon deploring the shortage of doctors. He said we would have to find ways and means of increasing the number of doctors. Of course we will. Let me point out, however, that the shortage of doctors occurred in Canada, not under a public medicare scheme but under a scheme where the doctors were private, individual businessmen. They have not been able to provide services to the people of this country where those services were required.

INDUSTRY-INSTRUCTIONS FROM U.S. RESPECTING FLOUR FOR CUBA
speechtext:
It
has come to my attention in recent days, Mr. Speaker, that Canadian political and economic sovereignty may be suffering an infringement-indeed, a violation-as the result of United States government policy respecting trade with the government of Cuba; and I take this opportunity to direct a query in this area to the Minister of Trade and Commerce or, in his absence, the Minister of Industry.
I am informed on excellent authority, sir, that directives have gone out to the three United States owned flour mills in Canada namely, Robin Hood, Quaker and Pillsbury, forbidding them to mill Canadian wheat in Canada for sale to Cuba. The order is articulated under the Trading with the Enemy Act, and apparently carries with it the implied threat of severe penalties for any offender.
I would add that so far as I am aware, these are not new directives, and this is not a new situation. On the contrary, the situation would appear to be a chronic or permanent, one. It has been the subject of widespread suggestion and speculation before. It has come freshly to light as a result of the $800 million wheat agreement that has just been concluded between Canada and the Soviet union.
The directive forbidding these three United States owned flour mills from processing wheat bound for Cuba has sat, I am informed, on the desks of the Canadian offices of these companies for a considerable time. I re-emphasize that so far as I am aware there is nothing new at the level of the directive itself. What is new, apparently, is that despite all the recent furore over United States government guidelines for foreign subsidiaries of domestic U.S. firms, and despite the insistence of the Canadian government that those guidelines have been modified to meet the legitimate principles of Canadian sovereignty, there has been no new directive rescinding the old one. The old one is still in effect, and is being observed once again in connection with the new Canada-Russia wheat deal.
Under the terms of this Canada-Russia deal, the Russians have purchased, for delivery over the next three years, about 45 millions bushels of wheat in the form of flour, and no one has attempted to make any secret of the fact that more than two thirds of it is earmarked for Cuba. The flour is
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion shipped in 100-pound bags, and the total 45 million-bushel purchase represents an annual sale of 6.6 million of these 100 pound bags.
The Russians are in process right now of placing their orders for the processing of this flour with mills in Canada, both Canadian-owned and American-owned, and the situation as I understand it is that while both Canadian-owned mills and American-owned mills are bidding on the orders destined for shipment via the west coast to Russia, only the Canadian-owned companies are bidding on the orders destined for shipment via the east coast to Cuba. The American-owned mills in this country are not bidding on the Cuban orders-presumably because of the old directives from their head offices in the United states which prevent them from doing so.
Now, there are two concessions with respect to this situation that I want to make immediately. The first is that the situation in no way interferes with Canadian business. On the contrary, in fact, it is a beneficial situation as far as the Canadian mills are concerned. They have the whole Cuban market to themselves, with no competition from the American-owned mills.
The second is that I am fully sympathetic with the interests of the United States government and the United States people in their courageous fight at this time-in Southeast Asia, in the Caribbean, in Europe and elsewhere-to resist the forces of aggression in Communist and other forms that threaten the free world. And I can fully appreciate their legitimate desire to withhold, wherever possible, any goods or materials which might be construed by them to be of help and comfort to their enemies.
But I submit, Mr. Speaker, that there is a principle at stake here and it is in the undeniable interest of our Canadian sovereignty that it be respected. Hon. members on the government side will say perhaps that no Canadian business is being hurt here; so, they will ask, what harm is being done?
But I would ask them this: What would happen if all the flour mills in Canada were American-owned? Then, would not the logical result be a situation wherein Canada would find that she could not sell any of her flour, or at least could not sell any flour to Cuba?
I would ask hon. gentlemen opposite this: Is the present situation with respect to the American-owned mills in this country in keeping with the spirit of good corporate Canadian citizenship? Is it in accord, in their
7608	COMMONS
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion view, with the principles of citizenship as they feel they should apply to individuals who live here, and make their living here?
I say only this, Mr. Speaker. These American-owned firms are here, and we are glad to have them here. But presumably some benefits accrue to them as a result of their being here and it is therefore incumbent upon them to fulfil the same responsibilities of citizenship in this country as we expect of individual persons who live here and work here.
For my part I believe these United States firms, left to their own social and corporate philosophies, do fulfil those responsibilities most admirably. It is only when a different authority interferes that there is the danger of trouble. In this case, sir, I submit that an over-riding authority has interfered and in so doing has not only inhibited the potential of these American-owned citizens of Canada, but has infringed upon Canadian political and economic sovereignty as well. If this is the visible part, what of the invisible part? I would ask the government to give us assurances that this is not the tip of an iceberg.

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert Winters (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: INDUSTRY-INSTRUCTIONS FROM U.S. RESPECTING FLOUR FOR CUBA
speechtext:
I am grateful to the hon. member for Winnipeg South for his remarks concerning a situation which would not, if it in fact exists, harmonize with good corporate Canadian citizenship.
[DOT] (10:10 p.m.)
When I learned of the hon. gentleman's question today we endeavoured to check with the companies concerned. We were able to communicate with most of them, and they said they have not received instructions not to sell any of this flour to Cuba. We propose to check with all of them and make sure of the facts in this regard.
The situation is as the hon. member represented it, that even if the American-owned companies were prevented from processing flour for Cuba, Canadian industry
DEBATES	July 12, 1366
would not lose because then Canadian-owned companies could process more of the wheat. In that way the Canadian economy will not suffer.
However, there is the question of the extension of extraterritoriality with which we were concerned in our meeting with the U.S. ministers earlier this year. Canadian ministers pressed our case very vigorously. We told them this was contrary to the best interests of Canada and totally incompatible with our concepts of Canadian sovereignty.
We told them we intended to take action to let Canadian companies know what we regarded to be good corporate Canadian citizenship. Hon. members know what the guiding principles are. We have set forth the principles under which we suggest that foreign and Canadian owned companies operate in all respects as good Canadian citizens.
We did leave it with the Americans, after pressing very vigorously, that if any cases came to our attention where there was any danger of infringement on Canadian sovereignty, we would bring them to their attention and pursue the matter, and if there is any evidence to that end, as a result of our approaches to these milling companies, we will certainly pursue it.
There have been one or two instances recently in which it was alleged that this sort of thing was happening. We took them up with the American authorities and we found out either it was not happening at all, or, if there was any shadow that it might be happening, appropriate action was taken to prevent it. I would like to assure the hon. member that this matter will be pursued along the lines I have mentioned, and I wish to thank him for bringing it to our attention.
